```{r}
#| label: setup
#| echo: false
#| output: false
root <- normalizePath("..")
inputs <- file.path(root, "02.inputs")
outputs <- file.path(root, "03.outputs")
derived <- file.path(inputs, "derived")

easypackages::packages("flextable", "ggplot2", "ggrepel", "ggspatial", "knitr",
                       "MASS", "modifiedmk", "patchwork", "rmarkdown", "sf",
                       "terra", "tools", prompt = FALSE)

# Write figures into the committed outputs folder rather than the render
# sidecar. With embed-resources the sidecar is deleted once its contents are
# inlined into the HTML, which leaves no PNG on disk for the README to show.
# Writing them here keeps a copy that survives the render and is in the
# repository.
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.path = file.path("..", "03.outputs", "figures", "mfig-"))
source(file.path(root, "05.scripts", "analysis_functions.R"))

# House table format: 9 pt, centred headers, numeric right, text left, single
# line spacing. Every table goes through fmt_tbl, so the house style is defined
# once and cannot drift between tables.
fmt_tbl <- function(df, right = NULL) {
  right_cols <- union(names(df)[vapply(df, is.numeric, TRUE)], right)
  left_cols <- setdiff(names(df), right_cols)
  ft <- flextable::flextable(df)
  ft <- flextable::fontsize(ft, size = 9, part = "all")
  ft <- flextable::align(ft, align = "center", part = "header")
  if (length(right_cols))
    ft <- flextable::align(ft, j = right_cols, align = "right", part = "body")
  if (length(left_cols))
    ft <- flextable::align(ft, j = left_cols, align = "left", part = "body")
  ft <- flextable::line_spacing(ft, space = 1, part = "all")
  ft <- flextable::padding(ft, padding.top = 1, padding.bottom = 1, part = "all")
  flextable::set_table_properties(ft, layout = "autofit", width = 1)
}

# Read a value out of a two-column item/value table by name. Stops rather than
# returning empty, so a renamed row breaks the render instead of silently
# emptying a sentence.
lookup <- function(tbl, item) {
  v <- tbl$value[tbl$item == item]
  if (length(v) != 1) stop("no unique row for: ", item)
  v
}
n_fmt <- function(x) format(as.numeric(x), big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE)

# The three timeseries, named once. Everything downstream reads these labels rather
# than repeating them, so the version and the input resolution attached to a
# series cannot drift between a table and the sentence describing it.
SERIES <- c(s1 = "S1: FWI1987, 13:00 observation",
            s2 = "S2: FWI2025, 13:00 observation",
            s3 = "S3: FWI2025, hourly observation")
# The same three timeseries as they are named inside a sentence, where a table
# label with its code and colon would not read.
SERIES_PROSE <- c(s1 = "FWI1987 on the 13:00 observation",
                  s2 = "FWI2025 on the 13:00 observation",
                  s3 = "FWI2025 on hourly weather")
# Station names arrive from the data mart in capitals; prose uses title case,
# keeping the RS suffix (ranger station) as the service writes it.
station_prose <- function(x) {
  x <- tools::toTitleCase(tolower(x))
  x <- gsub("\\bRs\\b", "RS", x)
  gsub("\\bMccuddy\\b", "McCuddy", x)
}

# The record's extent is read here, before it is described anywhere, so that no
# sentence in this document states a period the data do not cover.
cover <- read.csv(file.path(derived, "fwi-station-season-coverage.csv"),
                  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
kept <- subset(cover, status == "kept")
n_kept <- nrow(kept)
n_stations_kept <- length(unique(kept$station_name))
yr_first <- min(kept$year); yr_last <- max(kept$year)
n_seasons <- length(unique(kept$year))
```

# Introduction {#sec-intro}

British Columbia recorded the most severe wildfire seasons of its last century within the past two decades. In 2003 lightning and human causes produced more than 2,500 wildfire starts in the Interior, 334 homes were destroyed and more than 45,000 people were evacuated [@filmon2004firestorm, p. 10], after southern British Columbia had gone through "its driest three-year period on record" [@filmon2004firestorm, p. 17]. In 2017 more than 1.2 million hectares burned, about 65,000 people were displaced, suppression cost more than 568 million dollars and the provincial state of emergency lasted 70 days, the first declared since 2003 [@abbott2018newnormal, p. 25], and @kirchmeieryoung2019attribution found that human-induced climate change had made the fire weather and fire behaviour metrics of that season 2 to 4 times more likely and had increased the area burned by a factor of 7 to 11. More than 1.2 million hectares burned again in 2018 [@hessburg2019resilience, p. 7], the heat dome of late June 2021 accounted for 21 to 34 per cent of the area burned in North America that year, including 0.7 million hectares in British Columbia [@jain2024heatdome], and the 2023 Canadian season burned about 15 million hectares under May to October temperatures 2.2 °C above the 1991 to 2020 average [@jain2024canada2023]. @parisien2023abrupt placed four of the most severe British Columbia seasons of the last century in 2017, 2018, 2021 and 2023.

Those seasons followed a century in which burning had declined, and the historical record names several triggers for both the decline and the reversal. Tree-ring studies of the province's dry forests reconstructed the regime before suppression. In Douglas-fir and ponderosa pine forests of the southern interior, @heyerdahl2012mixed found a mean plot-composite fire scar interval of 21 years from 1700 to 1900 and a mixed-severity regime at 66 per cent of plots, and in central British Columbia @brookes2021disrupted found that 23 fires between 1619 and 1943 burned at intervals of 10 to 30 years, whereas current fire-free intervals of 70 to 180 years exceed the historical maximum. Drought was the trigger those records share. @chavardes2021drought found that below-average precipitation and summer drought synchronised fires across 14 dry-forest study areas of the Montane Cordillera from 1746 to 1945, and @harvey2017interannual found in west central British Columbia from 1600 to 1900 that drought increasingly synchronised fire from local to regional scales while the El Niño Southern Oscillation, the Pacific Decadal Oscillation and the Pacific North American pattern had a weak or inconsistent influence, except in years when the first two were both positive. People were a second trigger, acting in both directions. At Ne Sextsine in T'exelc territory, @copesgerbitz2022indigenous found that high fire frequency in low-severity plots ceased in the 1870s, following the smallpox epidemic, forced relocation to reserves and the prohibition of Indigenous burning, and @copesgerbitz2022governance traced five eras of provincial fire governance in which government decision-making superseded First Nations fire governance from the 1870s onward. @chavardes2021drought attributed the fall in fire occurrence and synchrony after 1945 to fire exclusion, suppression and climatic variation.

The instrumental record showed the same decline and then its end. @meyn2010spatial found that annual wildfire extent and occurrence across 16 landscape regions of British Columbia fell from 1920 to 2000 and that the fall was significantly related to wetter summers, and @meyn2010oscillations found that year-to-year fire variability in the province's biogeoclimatic zones over the same period was better related to summer drought than to climate oscillations. @parisien2023abrupt, analysing mapped fire perimeters and annual climate from 1919 to 2021, found that fire activity increased from 2005 onward after a century-long decline, as rapid warming raised moisture deficits even where precipitation remained high. Remote sensing and national fire records agree on the direction. @coops2018burned mapped burned area from Landsat for 1985 to 2015 and found a significant increase of 2.4 per cent per year, 709.3 hectares per year, in the Montane Cordillera ecozone, and @hanes2019regime found across Canada from 1959 to 2015 that area burned and the number of large fires had increased, that lightning-caused fires were increasing in most of western Canada while human-caused fires were stable or declining, and that the fire season had begun about one week earlier and ended about one week later. Across boreal forests, @gao2026distinct separated satellite-detected fires from 2002 to 2022 into natural and human causes and found that human-caused fires declined significantly over that period while natural fires were relatively stable. Lightning itself showed no clear trend. @aftergood2022lightning found a non-significant overall decrease in lightning-caused fires across western Canada from 1981 to 2018 and no trend in their clustering in British Columbia, although @wierzchowski2002lightning had shown that lightning is far more effective at igniting fire in British Columbia, with one fire for every 50 discharges against one for every 1,400 in Alberta. The provincial reviews and syntheses gave more weight to fuel and insects than the statistical studies could test. The review of the 2003 season held that "a successful record of fire suppression has led to a fuel buildup in the forests of British Columbia" [@filmon2004firestorm, p. 6], the review of 2017 found that the mountain pine beetle "was in many ways at the heart of 2017 wildfires" [@abbott2018newnormal, p. 11], and @daniels2011climate argued from the East Kootenay that the effects of climate change on fire may be exacerbated by land use, fire exclusion and beetle outbreaks. Against those views, @hessburg2019resilience concluded that in British Columbia "burned area is primarily controlled by annual to decadal climate and fire weather; fuels are typically not limiting" [@hessburg2019resilience, p. 7], and @romualdi2023mpb, in a meta-analysis of studies published from 2000 to 2021, found limited consensus on whether beetle outbreaks amplified or dampened later fire, with the answer depending on spatial scale, fuels and weather.

Where those studies rated fire danger rather than fire, they rated it with the Canadian Forest Fire Weather Index System, specified by @vanwagner1987fwi, implemented from the FORTRAN listing of @vanwagner1985fortran, and used operationally throughout Canada since 1970 [@cffdg2025fwi2025, p. 3]. @girardin2009summer approximated its Drought Code from monthly data for 1901 to 2002 and found that summer moisture explained 63 per cent of the variance in Canada-wide annual area burned from 1959 to 1999. @woolford2014lightning found significant increases in lightning-caused fire risk from 1963 to 2009 in two ecoregions of northwestern Ontario, associated with temperature and fire danger rating index anomalies. @jain2017seasonlength computed the System from the North American Regional Reanalysis for 1979 to 2015 and found that potential fire season length increased over large areas of North America and that trends in spread days and in the 99th percentile of the Fire Weather Index were mostly positive where significant. @jolly2015global, using three reanalyses and three danger indices, found that fire weather seasons lengthened across 25.3 per cent of the Earth's vegetated surface from 1979 to 2013. Station records in Europe and California, computed with the Fire Weather Index or with other danger indices, showed the same direction. @wastl2012climate computed the Fire Weather Index and other danger indices from daily observations at 25 stations in six Alpine countries from 1951 to 2010 and found significant increases in the Western and Southern Alps, together with more days above a predefined threshold, but only a weak increase in the Northern Alps and no clear signal in the inner Alpine valleys. @collins2014fire found fairly strong upward trends in high to extreme fire weather over 40 years at five stations in the northern Sierra Nevada, particularly after the mid-1990s, and @collins2025decreasing, returning to that region, found that fire season days below the 80th and 50th percentiles of the Energy Release Component had declined from the late 1990s and early 2000s. @trnka2021observed found an increasing frequency of fire weather days over most of the Czech Republic from 1956 to 2015, with the trends accelerating after 2000, @giannaros2023changes found that extreme fire weather days in Europe had become more frequent, with change-points in the Mediterranean around the late 1990s and the mid-2000s, and @drobyshev2021trends found a trend towards higher Monthly Drought Code values in April and May in the western and northern European boreal zone over 1901 to 2017. Most of those trends were counts of days beyond a threshold, whether a fixed index value, as in @wastl2012climate, or a percentile, as in @collins2025decreasing and in the 95th percentile of the Daily Severity Rating that @calheiros2020evolution used to define extreme fire weather days on the Iberian Peninsula. For the Okanagan itself, @nitschke2008okanagan used the Canadian Forest Fire Danger Rating System under several climate scenarios to project a 30 per cent longer fire season and a 95 per cent increase in summer fire weather severity in the North Okanagan by 2070, and @haughian2012climate expected the southern interior to "experience the most significant increases in fire indices" [@haughian2012climate, p. 6] of any part of the province. Every one of those studies predates the 2025 update, so the Canadian fire danger trends they report, observed or projected, are statements about the 1987 System.

The same studies show that how the System is computed changes what it reports. @jain2017seasonlength truncated their Canadian series because the reanalysis ceased to assimilate Canadian precipitation observations after 2002, and @venalainen2014europe computed European Fire Weather Index trends separately for the ERA-40 and ERA-Interim reanalyses, finding no obvious trend for 1960 to 1999 and a significant increase in southern and eastern Europe for 1980 to 2012. The input approximation matters as much as the input source. On the Iberian Peninsula, @herrera2013daily found that computing the Fire Weather Index from daily mean rather than 12 UTC instantaneous weather gave an Initial Spread Index about half as large and missed 45 per cent of the extreme days in the instantaneous series, and @bedia2012reanalysis found that three reanalyses all tended to underestimate the index computed at seven Spanish weather stations. At global scale, @field2020gfwed found that components computed from the MERRA-2 reanalysis were in general biased low against station data, and @vitolo2020era5 found that the ERA5 fire danger reanalysis showed higher biases "in mountainous areas" [@vitolo2020era5, p. 6]. In the mountains of Colorado, @silver2025colorado found no significant trend in the Hot-Dry-Windy Index in 22 years of tower observations, whereas the ERA5 reanalysis showed strong increasing trends across the state. The start of the calculation matters as well, since @mcelhinny2020era5 showed that overwintering the Drought Code rather than restarting it at 15 changed the number and distribution of fire spread days. The nearest designs to a version comparison compared different indices or different hours on one record. @matthews2009comparison found that three fire danger systems with similar structures gave "widely varying assessments of fire danger for a given set of inputs" [@matthews2009comparison, p. 41], and that on thirteen years of station data from Camden, New South Wales, the differences partly cancelled when each system used its own observation time and moisture sub-models, @dowdy2010sensitivity found on eight years of gridded Australian data that the McArthur Forest Fire Danger Index was less sensitive to wind and rain and more sensitive to temperature and humidity than the Fire Weather Index, and @rodell2024hourly compared an hourly Fire Weather Index with the standard daily index on the same numerical weather forecast for western North America and found that hourly values at noon were biased low because "standard noon local time usually does not coincide with the timing of peak fire behavior" [@rodell2024hourly, p. 931]. None of those studies compared the trend of one index under two versions of its own calculation.

Climate science has faced the same problem in other records and treats it as a question of homogeneity. @vose2012ushcn found that a change from afternoon to morning observation at about 20 per cent of the United States Historical Climatology Network stations imposed an artificial decrease of 0.20 °C on the national temperature trend, and @bengtsson2004reanalysis found that the ERA-40 warming trend of 0.14 K per decade for 1958 to 2001 fell to 0.10 K per decade once changes in the observing system were accounted for. @thorne2010reanalysis argued that reanalyses carried time-varying biases that at best reduce their utility for long-term trend monitoring, @venema2012homogenization benchmarked the algorithms used to remove such breaks from station networks, and @santer2000trenddiff showed that testing the trend in the difference between two temperature data sets found significant trend differences in about 30 per cent of pairs, mainly from differences in measurement system. @tsinko2018comparisons found the same problem in the Fire Weather Index itself, in that computing the System from raw and homogenised weather at 16 Canadian stations showed that homogenising the 66-year records lowered index values by about 0.7 to 8.4 per cent and reversed the long-term trend at some stations, among them Kapuskasing. The formulation of an index moves its trend in the same way. @vicenteserrano2010spei found that under imposed warming only the drought indices that included evapotranspiration showed an increase in drought severity, @tory2024sensitivity found that the temperature and humidity functions inside 16 fire danger and fire spread models turned three hypothetical climate change scenarios into projections ranging from minimal change to an increase of more than 50 per cent, with non-trivial differences even between models designed for similar fuels, and @dunn2022reference found that changing the reference period of a percentile index changed trends computed from the same data over the same years by 25 to 50 per cent. Percentile indices carry a further inhomogeneity of their own, since @zhang2005percentile showed that counts above a threshold set from a base period are biased at its boundaries and can show a trend in data that have none.

In 2025 the Canadian Forest Service Fire Danger Group replaced the 1987 System. The successor, which that report labelled FWI2025 to keep it distinct from FWI1987 [@cffdg2025fwi2025], was not a recalibration. The first of the key updates its executive summary listed was "Using hourly weather to better reflect maximum burning conditions" [@cffdg2025fwi2025, p. 2], and section 4.1.1 stated that "the time lag function used in the FWI2025 for the FFMC has been cut in half" [@cffdg2025fwi2025, p. 19]. The System now runs on an hourly stream, takes latitude, longitude and date so that daylight length enters the moisture calculation, and adopted the Initial Spread Index of the Fire Behaviour Prediction System [@fcfdg1992fbp] in place of the original.

Alongside those changes the report made a claim of continuity. Section 4.1 said that "an FFMC of 91 in FWI1987 should correspond to an FFMC of approximately 91 in FWI2025", and that deviations "should reflect meaningful differences in fuel moisture content" [@cffdg2025fwi2025, p. 18]. Read as written the claim was about levels, and it was plausible, because the update was designed so that a number on the old scale means roughly what it used to mean.

The difficulty is that fire danger trends are almost never reported as levels but as counts of days above a threshold, as seasonal severity accumulated over a season, or as the frequency of an extreme, as the studies above show. Those are properties of the upper tail, and a change that leaves a distribution's centre alone can still move its tail. Halving a drying time lag does exactly that, because it lets the litter layer respond further within a day, which widens the diurnal swing without necessarily shifting the daily mean. @herrera2013daily found that summarising the input weather as daily means missed 45 per cent of the extreme days, and if the version change widens the tail in a comparable way, an extreme-day count computed under FWI2025 will trend at a different rate from the same count computed under FWI1987, and every published Canadian fire danger trend becomes version-contingent in a way that had not been quantified.

Testing that is not straightforward, because FWI1987 and FWI2025 differ in two respects at once. FWI1987 takes a single daily observation at 13:00 local daylight time. FWI2025 "calculations always use hourly weather" [@cffdg2025fwi2025, pg. 8] and offered three input pathways, ranked in that report as best, good and usable [@cffdg2025fwi2025, p. 7], namely direct hourly observations, daily maxima and minima, and the legacy 13:00 observation. Running the old system on noon data against the new system on hourly data therefore confounds the version change with the input change, and a difference found that way could not be attributed to either, which is the situation @matthews2009comparison met when differences between systems cancelled once each used its own observation time.

This study separated them. Three danger series were computed from one hourly weather record for one basin, FWI1987 driven by the 13:00 observation, FWI2025 driven by the same 13:00 observation through the report's pathway C, and FWI2025 driven by the observed hourly weather through pathway A. The first contrast moved the version and held the input fixed, the second moved the input and held the version fixed, and the third was the contrast an agency actually faces when it migrates, which is the sum of the other two. @tbl-expectations sets out what the literature above led the study to expect for each metric family.

| Metric family | Expected direction | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Mean Fire Weather Index and seasonal severity rating | Positive trend in all three series; small difference in level between versions | Rising moisture deficits after 2005 [@parisien2023abrupt]; comparability of levels claimed in section 4.1 of @cffdg2025fwi2025 |
| Days above absolute thresholds, FFMC 91, FWI 19 and FWI 30 | Positive trend; steeper under FWI2025 than FWI1987; input resolution also moves the count | Halved Fine Fuel Moisture Code time lag [@cffdg2025fwi2025]; extreme days sensitive to how the input weather is summarised [@herrera2013daily; @rodell2024hourly] |
| Days above each series' own 90th and 95th percentiles | Positive trend; little difference between series; bias outside the base period | Percentile thresholds move with the series [@zhang2011indices]; base-period inhomogeneity [@zhang2005percentile; @dunn2022reference] |
| Daily lightning, person-caused and all-cause ignitions | Positive association with daily danger; weaker for lightning without strike data | Daily fire occurrence in British Columbia [@magnussen2012bc]; strike data in lightning occurrence models [@wotton2005lightning] |

: Expected direction of each metric family and the literature it rests on. {#tbl-expectations}

Three questions were asked. The first asked what the `r yr_first` to `r yr_last` trend in seasonal fire danger in the Okanagan basin was under each series, estimated identically. The second asked whether the three series gave different trends, and if so whether the difference lay in the version or in the input resolution. The prediction under test was specific and had two ways to fail. Under thresholds fixed in absolute index units, the faster-drying FWI2025 should widen the upper tail and produce a steeper positive slope in extreme-day counts than FWI1987, whereas under thresholds set as percentiles internal to each series over a common reference period that difference should largely vanish, because a percentile threshold moves with the series it is computed from. Divergence under both schemes, or under neither, would refute the mechanism rather than support it. The third asked whether any of the three predicted daily ignition counts better than the others, and whether the relationship between danger and ignition was stationary across the record.

The Okanagan basin was a suitable place to ask. It is a populated, fire-prone valley in the southern interior of British Columbia, the part of the province @haughian2012climate expected to see the largest increases in fire indices, with a long instrumented fire weather record, and its terrain is steep enough that a station record is preferable to a reanalysis whose fire danger biases are largest in mountainous areas [@vitolo2020era5]. The study detected change and did not attribute it, in that nothing here separated a change in fire danger from its causes, and no claim about anthropogenic forcing was made or implied.

The paper is organised as follows. @sec-data describes the basin, the two versions of the System, the hourly weather record and the ignition record. @sec-methods sets out the three-series design, the index computation and its checks, the seasonal metrics and thresholds, and the trend, slope-difference and ignition models. @sec-results reports the implementation checks, the position of each threshold in each series, the mechanism, the trends, the slope differences and the ignition skill. @sec-discussion interprets the opposing directions of the two changes and states what the record can and cannot resolve, and @sec-conclusions closes.

The study area was the `r sa("watershed_group_name")` watershed group of the British Columbia Freshwater Atlas, `r n_fmt(sa("basin_area_ha"))` ha in the southern interior of British Columbia, shown in @fig-study-area, with relief from `r n_fmt(sa("dem_min_elev_m"))` m at the valley floor to `r n_fmt(sa("dem_max_elev_m"))` m on the flanking uplands.

Three official boundaries carry the name Okanagan and they disagree by a factor of two, so the choice is stated. The provincial major watershed WA2 "Okanagan River" [@geobc2026majorwatersheds] measured 1,554,467 ha only because it annexes the Similkameen, a separate valley joined to it in that layer because the Similkameen reaches the Okanogan River in Washington State rather than because it drains to Okanagan Lake. The federal Water Survey of Canada sub-sub-drainage 08NM [@wsc2026subsubdrainage] measured 1,203,045 ha because 402,172 ha of it lies south of the international boundary. Within Canada the federal and provincial frameworks described the same basin to within 1.3 per cent. The study area was therefore the Freshwater Atlas group [@geobc2026fwagroups], the Canadian portion of the Okanagan watershed, entire.

The United States portion of the basin was out of scope by design and not by oversight, because the ignition record is the BC Wildfire Service incident set, the weather record is the BC Wildfire Service station network, and neither crosses the border, so a binational basin could not be measured with one consistent record. Every result below is for the Canadian basin and no inference is offered about the basin as a whole.

## Fire Danger Systems

Since 1970 fire danger in Canada has been rated with the Canadian Forest Fire Weather Index System [@cffdg2025fwi2025], one part of the Canadian Forest Fire Danger Rating System. @stocks1989overview described that rating system as four modules, "the now familiar Canadian Forest Fire Weather Index (FWI) System, the recently introduced Canadian Forest Fire Behavior Prediction (FBP) System, a proposed Canadian Forest Fire Occurrence Prediction (FOP) System, and the incomplete Accessory Fuel Moisture System" [@stocks1989overview, p. 451], the last intended to carry fuel-specific moisture codes for fuels such as cured grass and deciduous leaf litter. @taylor2006science later described two primary subsystems, the Fire Weather Index System and the Fire Behaviour Prediction System [@fcfdg1992fbp]. The two divide the problem in a way that matters for this study. The Fire Weather Index System rates the weather against one standard fuel, since "FWI1987 was designed to track conditions in a generalized pine forest (similar to C-3)" [@cffdg2025fwi2025, p. 3], whereas the Fire Behaviour Prediction System turns those ratings into spread rate and intensity for a mapped fuel type. Fire danger was measured here with the first of the two, in both of the versions now in circulation, and because the two versions are not interchangeable every value below carries its version.

FWI1987 is the System specified by @vanwagner1987fwi. Its six components are three fuel moisture codes, the Fine Fuel Moisture Code, the Duff Moisture Code and the Drought Code, and three fire behaviour indices built from them, the Initial Spread Index, the Buildup Index and the Fire Weather Index. A seventh quantity, the Daily Severity Rating, is a power transform of the Fire Weather Index and accumulates over a season into the seasonal severity rating. Its weather inputs are air temperature, relative humidity, ten-metre open wind speed and 24 hour rainfall [@lawson2008weather], taken from one observation per day at 13:00 local daylight time. No reference period normalises it, because the codes are a bookkeeping system carried from day to day, so a value depends on the whole preceding sequence and not only on the day it describes.

FWI2025 [@cffdg2025fwi2025] kept those components and changed how they were computed. The Fine Fuel Moisture Code was calculated hourly, on a modification of the diurnal method of @vanwagner1977hourly, with the drying time lag halved, and under the right conditions it continued to dry overnight. The report grounded that change in field moisture data, stating that "Observations of litter moisture from the field have suggested that the drying rate in the FFMC model itself is too slow" [@cffdg2025fwi2025, p. 19] and citing the diffusivity experiments of @anderson1990diffusivity, which found response times of 0.2 to 37 hours in recently dead fine fuels and 0.5 to 10 hours in weathered ones. The field evidence that litter moisture departs from the standard code is older than the update. @wotton2007standspecific analysed litter moisture sampled at sites across Canada from 1939 to 1961 and found that forest type, stand density, season and duff moisture each changed the relation between the Fine Fuel Moisture Code and surface litter moisture, and fitted a model adjusting the standard code for them. Outside Canada, @zhang2017hourlyffmc found that the standard hourly code underestimated dead fine fuel moisture in larch, Scots pine and oak stands of the Great Xing'an Mountains of China, while a locally calibrated version fitted with R^2^ from 0.920 to 0.969, and @alves2024portugal found from field measurements of maritime pine litter in central Portugal from 2014 to 2023 that correcting the code to field moisture raised the indices under dry conditions but did not improve the prediction of fire numbers or burned area. Canopy interception of the first 0.5 mm of rain became cumulative within a rain event and reset after six rain-free hours rather than at the end of each day, and the same six hour constant governed the 1.5 mm and 2.8 mm effective rainfall thresholds of the Duff Moisture Code and the Drought Code. Those two codes were also computed hourly, drying only between sunrise and sunset, with sunrise and sunset derived from latitude, longitude and date. The Initial Spread Index took the Fire Behaviour Prediction System wind function [@fcfdg1992fbp], which limits the effect of winds above 40 km h^-1^. The Buildup Index, the Fire Weather Index and the Daily Severity Rating were unchanged in form.

Three further components bear on how either version is run, and this study used or set aside each of them. The first is the overwintered Drought Code. @hanes2023drought found in instrumented plots in Alberta and Ontario that the Drought Code "predicted the moisture content of the deeper organic layers (10–18 cm depths) well" [@hanes2023drought, p. 836], and described the overwintering procedure that adjusts its spring starting value from the previous fall value and the overwinter precipitation. The 2025 report recommended that calculations continue until three consecutive days with a maximum temperature below 5 °C, which removes the need to estimate the carry-over fraction, and that where "the agency weather station network does not calculate the FWI System up to this date" an alternate weather stream such as "a nearby Environment and Climate Change Canada (ECCC) station" be used [@cffdg2025fwi2025, pp. 50–51]. This study restarted the code each spring, for the reason given under the startup rules below. The second is the fire season start rule, taken up under the season window below. The third is the grassland components. FWI2025 added optional grassland codes built on grass moisture models for standing and matted cured grass, together with two new optional inputs, solar radiation and curing [@cffdg2025fwi2025, pp. 13, 23], extending a line of work that includes the matted cured grass moisture model that @kidnie2015grass developed and tested in southern Ontario tallgrass prairie. The grassland and peatland components were excluded here, because this is a forest baseline and the two versions were compared only where they overlap.

Fuel type enters the Fire Behaviour Prediction System and not the Fire Weather Index System. In British Columbia the provincial fuel type layer described by @perrakis2018bcfueltypes was assembled from the Vegetation Resource Inventory into a dataset of "over 4.7 million VRI polygons" covering more than 94 million hectares [@perrakis2018bcfueltypes, p. 3], each assigned to a fuel type by rule, and its authors cautioned that "the FBP fuel typing process is inherently subjective, and the vegetation communities of BC frequently fall through the cracks between the FBP fuel types" [@perrakis2018bcfueltypes, p. 2]. For this basin the author built a fuel type map from the 2020 Vegetation Resource Inventory with that rule set, together with the stand-adjusted fine fuel moisture model of @wotton2007standspecific and a Fire Behaviour Prediction System run for single days in the summer of 2021 on gridded daily weather, in unpublished prototype work [@murphy2022cffdrsprototype], and that work is the reason the present study held fuel fixed. A trend in the Fire Weather Index System is a trend in the weather rated against one standard fuel, and a trend in fire behaviour across the basin's fuel types would need a fuel map for every season of the record, which this study did not build.

## Weather Record

```{r}
#| label: weather-record
#| echo: false
#| output: false
stn_tbl <- read.csv(file.path(derived, "station-metadata.csv"),
                    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
# The catalogue attributes of the five basin stations, as retrieved with the
# study area, and the retrieval log of the hourly archive. The sentences
# describing the network read these rather than restating them.
stn_cat <- sf::st_drop_geometry(sf::st_read(
  file.path(inputs, "spatial", "study-area.gpkg"), "stations", quiet = TRUE))
stn_cat$install_year <- as.integer(substr(stn_cat$INSTALL_DATE, 1, 4))
first_seen <- tapply(cover$year[cover$status != "station not reporting"],
                     cover$station_name[cover$status != "station not reporting"], min)
stn_cat$first_season <- as.integer(first_seen[stn_cat$STATION_NAME])
stn_cat <- stn_cat[order(stn_cat$install_year, stn_cat$STATION_NAME), ]
all_first_in_install_year <- all(stn_cat$first_season == stn_cat$install_year)
stn_list <- paste(sprintf("%s (station %d, %s m, installed %s)",
                          station_prose(stn_cat$STATION_NAME), stn_cat$STATION_CODE,
                          n_fmt(stn_cat$ELEVATION), stn_cat$install_year),
                  collapse = ", ")
stn_list <- sub(", ([^,]+ \\(station [^)]*\\))$", ", and \\1", stn_list)
retrieval <- read.csv(file.path(derived, "fire-weather-retrieval-log.csv"))
```

The weather record was the BC Wildfire Service weather data mart [@bcws2026datamart], a public directory of hourly observations from the provincial fire weather station network. It was used in preference to a gridded reanalysis for two reasons. It carries genuinely hourly precipitation, without which pathway A cannot be run as specified rather than approximated, and @cffdg2025fwi2025 states the caveat that a reanalysis would have imposed on this basin directly, that "numerical weather model outputs are not strictly the same as point observations of weather from a weather station. At the grid cell scale, outputs from numerical models typically represent what can be thought of as average conditions across that cell." A cell of roughly nine kilometres across terrain running from `r n_fmt(sa("dem_min_elev_m"))` m to `r n_fmt(sa("dem_max_elev_m"))` m is a coarse instrument.

The stations belong to the BC Wildfire Service weather station network. Its catalogue record states that "BCWS operates a network of automated hourly reporting weather stations to support all aspects of fire management", that "The data are used as input to the Canadian Forest Fire Danger Rating System, as a basis for weather forecasting and for climate monitoring", and that "Sensors at the weather stations monitor temperature, relative humidity, wind speed and direction and rainfall" [@bcws2026stations]. The catalogue layer holds one point per actively reporting station, with a numeric station code, a name, a three-letter acronym, latitude, longitude, elevation and installation date. The `r nrow(stn_cat)` stations inside the basin were `r stn_list`, and `r if (all_first_in_install_year) "each first appeared in the archive in the season it was installed" else "not every station first appeared in the archive in the season it was installed"`. The hourly archive for those stations is the BC Wildfire Service weather data mart [@bcws2026datamart], which carries for every station and hour the observed precipitation, temperature, relative humidity, wind speed and wind direction, the hourly Fine Fuel Moisture Code, Initial Spread Index and Fire Weather Index, and once a day the daily precipitation and the six FWI1987 codes that the service computed operationally.

The record retrieved was every hourly observation from the `r sa("fire_weather_stations")` stations the BC Data Catalogue places inside the basin polygon [@bcws2026stations], for every season the data mart holds [@bcws2026datamart]. Seasons 1987 to 2023 are published as one province-wide file per year and seasons 2024 onward as one file per day, and both layouts were read in full and filtered to the basin stations, which kept `r n_fmt(sum(retrieval$rows_kept))` hourly observations out of `r n_fmt(sum(retrieval$rows_seen))` province-wide rows for the `r min(retrieval$year)` to `r max(retrieval$year)` seasons.

Timestamps in that archive are Local Standard Time, which was verified rather than assumed. The FWI1987 codes that BC Wildfire Service computed operationally appeared in the record at hour 12 and at no other hour, and because the standard fire weather observation is 13:00 local daylight time, hour 12 is 13:00 LDT and the stamp is Pacific Standard Time, UTC-8, year round. The modal hour of daily maximum temperature in summer fell where that reading implies.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-stations
#| tbl-cap: "The weather record. Coverage is the share of the 1 April to 30 September hours in which temperature, humidity and wind were all observed, before any gap filling. A season is kept when coverage reaches 95 per cent and no single gap exceeds 24 hours."
#| echo: false
tz <- read.csv(file.path(derived, "timezone-verification.csv"))

agg <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(cover, cover$station_name), function(d) {
  k <- subset(d, status == "kept")
  data.frame(
    Station = d$station_name[1],
    `Elevation (m)` = round(d$elevation_m[1]),
    Installed = stn_cat$install_year[match(d$station_name[1], stn_cat$STATION_NAME)],
    `First season` = ifelse(nrow(k), min(k$year), NA),
    `Last season` = ifelse(nrow(k), max(k$year), NA),
    `Seasons kept` = nrow(k),
    `Seasons dropped` = sum(d$status == "dropped, coverage"),
    `Not reporting` = sum(d$status == "station not reporting"),
    `Median coverage` = round(median(k$observed_fraction), 3),
    check.names = FALSE)
}))
agg <- agg[order(-agg$`Seasons kept`), ]
fmt_tbl(agg)
```

@tbl-stations gives the result. `r n_kept` station-seasons across `r n_stations_kept` stations survived, spanning `r yr_first` to `r yr_last`, `r n_seasons` distinct seasons. The daily codes appeared at hour 12 in `r n_fmt(tz$daily_codes_at_hour_12)` records and at other hours in `r tz$daily_codes_at_other_hours`, which is what fixed the convention. The modal hour of daily maximum temperature in summer was `r tz$modal_hour_of_max_temp_summer`:00 Local Standard Time, three hours after solar noon at this longitude, which is consistent with it.

```{r}
#| label: coverage-caption
#| echo: true
#| output: false
# The caption's counts are the same objects the station table reports.
n_dropped <- sum(cover$status == "dropped, coverage")
cov_cap <- sprintf(paste(
  "Station reporting by season. Each cell is one station-season, shaded by the",
  "share of the 1 April to 30 September hours in which temperature, humidity",
  "and wind were all observed; an outlined cell met the 95 per cent rule and",
  "was kept, a crossed cell was dropped for coverage, and a blank cell is a",
  "season in which the station did not report. %d station-seasons at %d",
  "stations were kept and %d dropped, over %d to %d."),
  n_kept, n_stations_kept, n_dropped, yr_first, yr_last)
# The two facts the sentence under the figure states, computed from the same
# table: the share of dropped seasons before 2000, and the first season each
# station reported at all.
n_dropped_pre2000 <- sum(cover$status == "dropped, coverage" & cover$year < 2000)
first_report <- tapply(cover$year[cover$status != "station not reporting"],
                       cover$station_name[cover$status != "station not reporting"], min)
late_station <- names(first_report)[which.max(first_report)]
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-coverage
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3.0
#| fig-dpi: 300
#| fig-cap: !expr cov_cap
# One row per station in elevation order, one cell per season, shaded by the
# share of the 1 April to 30 September hours observed. A kept season is outlined,
# a season dropped for coverage is crossed, and a season in which the station did
# not report is left blank, so the switch-on and switch-off pattern of the
# network is visible in a way the station table cannot show.
cv <- cover
cv$station <- station_prose(cv$station_name)
st <- unique(cv[, c("station", "elevation_m")]); st <- st[order(st$elevation_m), ]
yrs <- sort(unique(cv$year))
ramp <- colorRampPalette(c("#F7EFE6", "#1B4F72"))(101)
op <- par(mar = c(3.2, 8.4, 0.6, 0.8), oma = c(2.2, 0, 0, 0), mgp = c(2, 0.6, 0), cex = 0.75)
plot(NA, xlim = range(yrs) + c(-0.5, 0.5), ylim = c(0.5, nrow(st) + 0.5),
     xlab = "Season", ylab = "", yaxt = "n", xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i")
axis(2, at = seq_len(nrow(st)),
     labels = sprintf("%s, %d m", st$station, round(st$elevation_m)),
     las = 1, tick = FALSE)
for (i in seq_len(nrow(st))) for (y in yrs) {
  r <- cv[cv$station == st$station[i] & cv$year == y, ]
  if (!nrow(r) || r$status == "station not reporting") next
  rect(y - 0.5, i - 0.5, y + 0.5, i + 0.5,
       col = ramp[1 + round(100 * r$observed_fraction)], border = NA)
  if (r$status == "kept")
    rect(y - 0.5, i - 0.5, y + 0.5, i + 0.5, border = "grey20", lwd = 0.7)
  else points(y, i, pch = 4, cex = 0.55, col = "#943126")
}
par(xpd = NA)
legend(min(yrs) - 0.5, -0.35, horiz = TRUE, bty = "n", cex = 0.75,
       legend = c("kept, 95 per cent or more observed", "dropped for coverage",
                  "shading, share of hours observed, 0 (pale) to 1 (dark)"),
       pch = c(0, 4, 15), col = c("grey20", "#943126", "#1B4F72"),
       pt.cex = c(1.2, 0.7, 1.2))
par(op)
```

@fig-coverage shows what the table cannot, which is when each station reported. The network was switched on and off for operational reasons, so `r n_dropped_pre2000` of the `r n_dropped` dropped seasons fell before 2000, and the `r station_prose(late_station)` station reported only from `r max(first_report)`.

### Season Window

The window was a fixed calendar one, 1 May to 30 September, 153 days, with the calculation spun up from 1 April so that thirty days of weather preceded the first reported day.

That was a departure from the original design, which proposed the Canadian rule that section C-2.3 of @cffdg2025fwi2025 describes as the criterion most often used across Canada, to "start calculation three days after the disappearance of snow cover", or, where snow cover cannot be observed, after three days above 12 degrees Celsius [@lawson2008weather]. The rule was implemented, run, and abandoned, because these stations do not report through the winter, so the rule fired on whatever day a station was switched on, and the station reporting record above shows that the switch-on date varied by station and season for operational reasons. The same constraint has been met before. @field2015gfwed, building the Global Fire Weather Database, noted that data for their Canadian comparison stations "were available only for the fire season, which was determined using a temperature threshold" [@field2015gfwed, p. 1411], and @hanes2020overwinter, working with fire weather stations in Alberta and Ontario, took winter precipitation from nearby Environment and Climate Change Canada stations because "fire weather stations are not operated during the winter" [@hanes2020overwinter, p. 5].

One consequence was stated rather than repaired. Fire season length could not be estimated from this network and was therefore not among the metrics, although lengthening season is among the most-reported fire danger trends, because a network whose stations are switched on and off for operational reasons cannot measure when a season begins. The published definitions of the season answer different questions and fail in different ways on a record like this one. The weather rule of @lawson2008weather and @wotton1993seasonlength, which @mcelhinny2020era5 stated as a season "active on the fourth day following 3 consecutive days with a maximum temperature of 12 °C or higher" and over "after 3 consecutive days with a maximum temperature of 5 °C or lower" [@mcelhinny2020era5, p. 1826], dates the weather season and needs a record that runs through the shoulder months. @jolly2015global defined fire weather season length from the danger series itself, as "the number of days each year when fire danger is above half its value range" [@jolly2015global, p. 2], and found that it lengthened across 25.3 per cent of the Earth's vegetated surface from 1979 to 2013, a definition that dates the danger season and needs the stations to be reporting before the first such day. Definitions based on fires rather than weather date the fire season: @westerling2016increasing measured it from the first discovery to the last control of a large fire and found western United States forest fire seasons in 2003 to 2012 more than 84 days longer than in 1973 to 1982, @albertgreen2013timing dated its start and end where a smoothed daily lightning-fire risk curve crossed set thresholds in Alberta and Ontario, and @granville2026season dated it from observed wildfires across Ontario and found it lengthening by a median of about 0.5 days per year in the northwest. Those need a complete and well-dated ignition record, which @sec-data shows the basin's record is not after 2000. The metrics that remained here were counts and sums over a window of fixed length, which the network can measure, and what that window gives up is taken up in @sec-discussion.

### Data Limitation: Gaps and Startup

Runs of missing temperature, humidity or wind up to 24 hours were filled by linear interpolation, since the reference implementation requires a gap-free hourly stream, and missing precipitation was filled with zero, because rain cannot be invented. A station-season was kept only where at least 95 per cent of the 1 April to 30 September hours were observed and no single gap exceeded 24 hours.

Filling a gap with no rain makes a missing wet spell look dry and pushes danger up. The direction matters and is stated. Coverage in this record was worse early than late, so this bias, where it acted, inflated danger in early seasons and therefore worked against an increasing trend rather than for one. It was identical across the three series by construction, since all three ran on the same filled record, and so could not move a contrast between versions.

Each station-season started from FFMC 85, DMC 6 and DC 15, the values @vanwagner1987fwi gives and the reference implementation defaults to. The Drought Code was not overwintered, because these stations report no winter weather for an overwintering calculation to run on. That departs from provincial practice, since @hanes2020overwinter reported that "the western provinces regularly overwinter the DC" [@hanes2020overwinter, p. 2], adjusting the fall value by the precipitation received over winter. The departure matters for absolute counts. @mcelhinny2020era5 computed a global Fire Weather Index reanalysis for 1979 to 2018 both ways and found that "even a modest difference in FWI values at start-up can lead to important differences in the number and spatial distribution of fire spread days between the overwintered and default calculations" [@mcelhinny2020era5, p. 1829], illustrated with the 2016 season over North America, when fuel moisture before the Fort McMurray fire in Alberta followed low overwinter precipitation and severe fall drought. The Drought Code here therefore carried startup information into early May in every season, identically in all three series, and its effect on absolute Drought Code, Buildup Index and extreme-day levels is reported with the implementation checks in @sec-results.

## Fire Activity

```{r}
#| label: ignition-inputs
#| echo: false
#| output: false
ign_daily <- read.csv(file.path(derived, "ignitions-daily.csv"), stringsAsFactors = F)
ign_daily$date <- as.Date(ign_daily$date)
completeness <- read.csv(file.path(derived, "ignition-completeness.csv"),stringsAsFactors = F)
attribution <- read.csv(file.path(derived, "ignition-attribution.csv"), stringsAsFactors = F)

n_total_incidents <- sum(completeness$n_incidents)
n_dated <- sum(completeness$n_dated)
n_undated <- n_total_incidents - n_dated
pct_dated <- round(100 * n_dated / n_total_incidents, 1)

# Dating completeness by decade, computed here so the sentence below quotes the
# table rather than describing it from memory.
completeness$decade <- paste0(completeness$year %/% 10 * 10, "s")
cd_pre <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(completeness, completeness$decade), function(d)
  data.frame(decade = d$decade[1],
             pct_dated = 100 * sum(d$n_dated) / sum(d$n_incidents))))
cd_pre <- cd_pre[order(cd_pre$decade), ]
```

The ignition record was the BC Wildfire Service historical incident set [@bcws2026incidents], clipped to the basin, `r n_fmt(n_total_incidents)` incidents over the `r sa("first_year")` to `r sa("last_year")` seasons.

Two properties of that record governed what could be asked of it, and neither was repaired here, because neither can be. First, many incidents could not be placed on a day at all. `r n_fmt(n_dated)` of `r n_fmt(n_total_incidents)` incidents, `r pct_dated` per cent, carried an ignition date, and the remaining `r n_fmt(n_undated)` could not enter a daily series at any threshold. The missing dates were not spread evenly, and they did not concentrate where intuition puts them, in that the earliest decade in the record was `r round(head(cd_pre$pct_dated, 1), 0)` per cent dated and the most recent was `r round(tail(cd_pre$pct_dated, 1), 0)` per cent. Missing date and missing cause were largely the same records. Second, cause attribution was not stationary. @tbl-completeness gives both by decade, and a lightning-caused count that falls after 2000 may record a change in how cause was coded rather than a change in ignition.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-completeness
#| tbl-cap: "Completeness of the ignition record by decade. A dated incident can be placed on a day; an attributed incident carries a recorded cause. Both fall sharply after 2000 and the same records are usually missing both."
#| echo: true
completeness$decade <- paste0(completeness$year %/% 10 * 10, "s")
cd <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(completeness, completeness$decade), function(d) {
  data.frame(
    Decade = d$decade[1],
    Incidents = sum(d$n_incidents),
    Dated = sum(d$n_dated),
    `Dated %` = round(100 * sum(d$n_dated) / sum(d$n_incidents), 1),
    Attributed = sum(d$n_caused),
    `Attributed %` = round(100 * sum(d$n_caused) / sum(d$n_incidents), 1),
    check.names = FALSE)
}))
fmt_tbl(cd)
```

```{r}
#| label: ignition-caption
#| echo: true
#| output: false
# Season-by-cause counts and the two completeness measures, with the pooled
# shares before 2000 and from 2000 onward computed here for the caption.
ibs <- read.csv(file.path(derived, "ignitions-by-season.csv"),
                stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
cause_tab <- xtabs(n ~ fire_cause + fire_year, ibs)
cause_tab <- cause_tab[c("Lightning", "Person", "Unknown"), , drop = FALSE]
share <- function(rows, col) 100 * sum(completeness[[col]][rows]) / sum(completeness$n_incidents[rows])
ign_cap <- sprintf(paste(
  "Ignitions by season and the completeness of their records. Upper panel,",
  "incidents per season by reported cause, %s in all. Lower panel, the share",
  "of incidents carrying an ignition date and the share carrying a recorded",
  "cause, which were %.0f and %.0f per cent before 2000 and %.0f and %.0f per",
  "cent from 2000 onward. Both panels are the same records, so the fall in the",
  "lower panel is what makes the cause split in the upper panel unreadable as",
  "an ignition trend after 2000."),
  n_fmt(n_total_incidents),
  share(completeness$year < 2000, "n_dated"), share(completeness$year < 2000, "n_caused"),
  share(completeness$year >= 2000, "n_dated"), share(completeness$year >= 2000, "n_caused"))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-ignitions
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-dpi: 300
#| fig-cap: !expr ign_cap

# the study-area map uses; the lines are the two completeness measures from the
# same completeness table the decade table summarises.
cause_cols <- c(Lightning = "#1B7A5A", Person = "#B3242B", Unknown = "grey60")
yrs2 <- as.integer(colnames(cause_tab))
op <- par(mfrow = c(2, 1), mar = c(1.2, 4.2, 0.6, 1), oma = c(2.5, 0, 0, 0),

legend("bottomleft", legend = c("dated", "cause attributed"),
```

@fig-ignitions shows the same records season by season. The upper panel gives the counts by cause and the lower panel the two completeness measures, and the fall in the lower panel after 2000 is what makes the cause split in the upper panel unreadable as an ignition trend.

The design responded to both rather than caveating them. The ignition models below carry season as a fixed effect, so the danger coefficient is identified only from day-to-day variation inside a season. Reporting completeness and cause coding both change between seasons and neither changes within one, so a between-season contrast would confound the danger effect with the record keeping and a within-season contrast cannot. Three response series were modelled, lightning, person-caused and all causes together, because the all-cause series cannot be affected by cause coding at all and is therefore the one that decides when the three disagree. Because detection of small fires also improved over the record, every result was reported at three minimum sizes, no limit, one hectare and four hectares, and a conclusion that survived at only one threshold was reported as not surviving.

# Methods {#sec-methods}

## Study Design

FWI1987 and FWI2025 differ in version and in input resolution simultaneously, so comparing one against the other answers no question about either. Three series were computed from a single hourly weather record, and each contrast moved one thing (@tbl-design).

| Series | System  | Weather input               | Pathway                        |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| S1     | FWI1987 | daily 13:00 LDT observation | the legacy configuration       |
| S2     | FWI2025 | daily 13:00 LDT observation | pathway C of @cffdg2025fwi2025 |
| S3     | FWI2025 | observed hourly weather     | pathway A of @cffdg2025fwi2025 |

: The three fire danger series and what separates them. {#tbl-design}

S1 against S2 isolated the version change at fixed input, S2 against S3 isolated the input resolution change at fixed version, and S1 against S3 was the operational contrast an agency faces on migration, the sum of the other two. All three ran on the same weather, the same season window, the same startup values and the same gap filling, so nothing that differed between them was an artefact of the record.

Pathway C is the report's own procedure for the legacy observation. The 13:00 observation was converted to estimated daily maxima and minima using national constants, daily maximum temperature being about 2 degrees Celsius above the 13:00 value, minimum wind speed 10 per cent of it and maximum wind speed 30 per cent above it, and humidity carried through at constant vapour content; those maxima and minima were then expanded to an hourly stream by the sinusoidal method of @beck1989diurnal with the default offset and decay coefficients of Table A-1 of @cffdg2025fwi2025. Daily rainfall, whose timing is unknown in a once-daily observation, was placed at the first hour after sunrise, which is the rule the report gives and the rule FWI1987 implicitly used.

## Index Computation

FWI2025 was computed with the reference implementation published by the Canadian Forest Service Fire Danger Group [@nrcan2026cffdrsng], run unmodified at the version cited. It reproduced the standard output distributed with it exactly, to the last decimal place the file carries, over the 2,623 hour Petawawa Research Forest test record.

FWI1987 was implemented for this study in Python, so that both systems ran inside one process on one record, and the implementation was checked in two ways, both reported in the results. The first check was against the CRAN package `cffdrs`, version 1.9.2 [@wang2017cffdrs; @wang2026cffdrspkg], an independently published implementation maintained by the Canadian Forest Service, run through R over the same test record. The second was against the FWI1987 codes that BC Wildfire Service itself computed operationally at these stations at the time, which the data mart preserves alongside the raw observations, so that a different party, different code and a different decade met the same weather.

Two constants differ between @vanwagner1987fwi as printed and @vanwagner1985fortran as programmed, and this implementation followed the program. The moisture transform coefficient is 147.2772, not the rounded 147.2 of the report, since 59.5 x 250 / 101 = 147.27722772 is the value that closes the scale; and the Duff Moisture Code moisture functions take the listing's form. Using the rounded constants instead moved the Fine Fuel Moisture Code by up to 3.9 units over the test record, which would have entered a version comparison as a difference between systems when it is a difference between roundings.

## Seasonal Metrics

Six seasonal metrics were computed per station, season and series over the 1 May to 30 September window, namely mean Fire Weather Index, seasonal severity rating as the sum of the Daily Severity Rating, peak Buildup Index, and counts of days above each of the thresholds described next. Because FWI2025 produces an hourly value and FWI1987 a daily one, the FWI2025 series were summarised to a daily value at 16:00 Local Standard Time, which is 17:00 local daylight time. That hour is the conventional peak burn hour, and it is the modal hour of peak burning conditions in the reference implementation's own distributed output. It was not chosen from this record; for comparison, the modal hour of daily maximum summer temperature here was `r tz$modal_hour_of_max_temp_summer`:00 Local Standard Time. The daily maximum over all 24 hours was carried as a sensitivity and not as the primary, because the maximum of 24 draws exceeds a single daily value for reasons that have nothing to do with the version change.

The second question turns on the thresholding, so both schemes were built and neither was preferred.

Absolute thresholds are fixed numbers on the index scale applied unchanged to all three series, which is the scheme an agency uses, because a danger class is a number in a manual. @taylor2006science traced how Canadian danger classes were set from correlations between Fire Weather Index System values and historical fire occurrence, and reported that British Columbia defined its classes from the Fire Weather Index and the Buildup Index separately for three danger regions with different fire climates. Three thresholds were used. FFMC 91 was taken from section 4.1 of @cffdg2025fwi2025, so that counting days above it tested that report's comparability sentence directly, and it is also the value above which the Canadian Wildland Fire Information System classes the Fine Fuel Moisture Code as extreme [@field2015gfwed]. A Fire Weather Index above 30 is that system's extreme class [@field2015gfwed], and a Fire Weather Index above 19 is the fire spread day threshold of @podur2011spread, which @mcelhinny2020era5 used to count spread days in their global reanalysis. @field2015gfwed noted that such extreme thresholds "will be different in other regions" [@field2015gfwed, p. 1409], so the absolute counts here are Canadian classes applied to one basin and not local calibrations.

Relative thresholds are percentiles of each series' own distribution over a common reference period, taken as 1991 to 2020, the current World Meteorological Organization normal, and fixed before any metric was computed. Climate extremes monitoring moved to thresholds of this kind because, in the review of @zhang2011indices, "few physically based thresholds have relevance in all parts of the world" [@zhang2011indices], and @jain2017seasonlength used the 99th percentile of the Fire Weather Index alongside counts of spread days for North America. British Columbia uses a threshold of the same kind operationally, since the head fire intensity layer of the provincial strategic threat analysis "was developed using the 90th percentile fire weather index value for an interpolated and elevation-adjusted analysis of weather station values" [@bcws2026psta]. A day above a series' own 90th percentile means the same thing in each series by construction, so a difference in trend under relative thresholds cannot be an artefact of the two systems sitting at different levels.

Percentile counts carry two known problems. @zhang2005percentile showed by Monte Carlo simulation that sampling error in a threshold estimated from a fixed base period leads to "overestimated exceedance rates outside the base period" [@zhang2005percentile, p. 1641] and underestimated rates inside it, producing an artificial jump at the boundary, larger for higher percentiles and for positively autocorrelated observations, that a linear trend fitted across it reads as a trend, and they removed it with a bootstrap estimate of the in-base rates. That correction was applied here. For each season inside the 1991 to 2020 base period, the threshold was re-estimated with that season removed and each other base season in turn duplicated in its place, and the count for the season was the mean over those replacements, while the last `r yr_last - 2020` seasons, which lie outside the base period, used the threshold from the whole base period. @zhang2005percentile estimated a threshold for each calendar day, whereas the threshold here was estimated from all days of the season pooled, so the procedure was adapted from a daily to a seasonal threshold. @dunn2022reference then showed that trends computed from the same data over the same years differ when the reference period changes and the climate has shifted between the two periods, by about 1 day per decade, around 25 per cent, in the global HadEX3 warm-day index over 1961 to 2018 and by about 3 days per decade, around 50 per cent, at De Bilt [@dunn2022reference, p. 8]. That problem has no correction, because it is a property of the choice rather than an error in the estimate, so the reference period was fixed before any metric was computed and a relative-threshold trend here is a statement about the 1991 to 2020 period as well as about its index.

One property of that construction is stated because it resembles a result and is not one. Inside the reference period the mean number of days above a series' own 90th percentile is close to ten per cent of the days in it, in every series, by construction. The level of a relative count therefore carries no information about the version at all, and only its trend does.

Reference distributions were computed per station as well as per series, because pooling them would mix a valley station at `r round(min(stn_tbl$ELEVATION))` m with a ridge station at `r n_fmt(round(max(stn_tbl$ELEVATION)))` m, and the percentile would then describe the network rather than the site.

## Statistical Analysis

Trends were estimated with the non-parametric pairing that fire weather trend studies have adopted, the Theil-Sen slope with a Mann-Kendall test. @jain2017seasonlength applied that pairing to the potential fire season length and to the 99th percentile of the Fire Weather Index across North America from 1979 to 2015, computing the System from the North American Regional Reanalysis with field significance testing and a Canadian series truncated because the reanalysis ceased to assimilate Canadian precipitation observations after 2002, and @venalainen2014europe applied it to the Fire Weather Index over Europe from 1960 to 2012 with a Mann-Kendall test corrected for autocorrelation through an effective sample size, computing trends separately for the ERA-40 and ERA-Interim reanalyses. The Theil-Sen slope, the median of all pairwise slopes [@sen1968slope], was computed here over the `r n_seasons` seasons from `r yr_first` to `r yr_last` that survived the coverage rule, on the actual season numbers so that a gap in the sequence was honoured rather than treated as a step of one. The median of pairwise slopes was preferred to least squares because @hirsch1982trend showed that it was an unbiased estimator of a linear trend with considerably higher precision than a regression slope on highly skewed data, and seasonal counts of extreme days are skewed.

Significance was the Mann-Kendall test [@mann1945nonparametric] with the variance correction of @hamed1998mmk, which inflates the variance of the test statistic by the serial correlation present in the series rather than assuming independence. Serial correlation alters the variance of the Mann-Kendall statistic [@yue2002autocorrelation] and gives too large a rejection rate on trendless series [@bayazit2007prewhiten], and the literature offers four responses, prewhitening, trend-free prewhitening, variance correction and block bootstrap resampling [@onoz2012blockbootstrap]. Prewhitening was not used. @bayazit2007prewhiten found by simulation that it corrected the false rejection rate on trendless autocorrelated series but reduced the power of the test when a trend was present, and @yue2002autocorrelation showed that removing a positive serial correlation component by prewhitening also reduced the magnitude of the trend itself [see also @yue2002prewhitening]. The uncorrected result was reported alongside the corrected one only to show the size of the correction.

One approximation in that correction is stated here. Coverage dropped seasons out of the middle of some station records, so the season sequence was not evenly spaced. The Mann-Kendall statistic itself is unaffected, because it depends on the order of the values and not on their spacing, and the Theil-Sen slope was computed on the actual season numbers so a gap is a gap. The Hamed and Rao variance correction, however, estimates autocorrelation at lags counted in observations rather than in years, which across a gap compares seasons further apart than the lag says. The direction of that error is knowable, because it attributes to lag one a correlation measured over two or more years, which is smaller, so the correction applied was smaller than the true one and the test less conservative than it would be on a complete record. A marginal result is therefore weaker than its q value suggests.

Metric families were corrected within each series by the false discovery rate procedure of @benjamini1995fdr. The eight metrics in a family were computed from one series and rise and fall with the same fire weather, so their tests were not independent. @benjamini2001dependency proved that the same procedure still controls the false discovery rate when the test statistics have positive regression dependency on those of the true null hypotheses, which metrics driven by one weather record were expected to satisfy, and @wilks2016stippling showed by simulation that under moderate to strong correlation among tests the procedure becomes conservative rather than permissive. @wilks2016stippling also found that only 3 of the 281 papers published in the Journal of Climate in the first half of 2014, 1.1 per cent, considered multiple testing at all. Confidence intervals on a single slope were percentile intervals over 2,000 moving-block bootstrap resamples of seasons, with the block construction described next.

Comparing the trends of two records that share most of their variability has a precedent in the evaluation of atmospheric temperature data sets. @santer2000trenddiff tested the trend in the series of differences between two data sets rather than the overlap of their separate confidence intervals, because the difference removes variability common to both, and found that roughly 30 per cent of data set pairs differed significantly in lower tropospheric trend, mainly through differences in measurement system, where overlapping intervals had not shown it. @wilks1997resampling showed that applying the same resampling pattern to every element of a data vector carries the cross correlation between elements into the resampled statistics without the need to model it. The three series here came from one weather record and were strongly dependent, and each was also serially correlated from season to season. Resampling single seasons would keep the pairing between series but discard that serial correlation, which block bootstraps retain by resampling runs of consecutive observations [@kunsch1989bootstrap; @politis1994stationary], and @onoz2012blockbootstrap found that a block bootstrap Mann-Kendall test had power comparable with the other corrections for serial dependence. The difference between two series' slopes was therefore estimated by a moving-block bootstrap, drawing blocks of consecutive seasons with replacement and recomputing both slopes on the same resampled seasons in every one of 4,000 replicates, which kept the pairing between series by construction. Blocks were `r paste(sort(unique(vapply(as.integer(table(kept$station_name)[table(kept$station_name) >= 15]), block_length, integer(1)))), collapse = ' or ')` seasons long for station records of `r min(table(kept$station_name)[table(kept$station_name) >= 15])` to `r max(table(kept$station_name))` seasons, the cube root of the record length rounded up, which grows with the record but more slowly than it, as @kunsch1989bootstrap required for consistency, and they were drawn from the seasons in order of occurrence so that a gap in a station record fell inside a block. The interval on the difference was the plain percentile interval, on which the bias-corrected and accelerated interval of @efron1987better improves to second-order correctness [@diciccio1996bootstrap]. The two-sided p value was computed under the null hypothesis, following the first guideline of @hall1991guidelines, that resampling should reflect the null hypothesis, whose violation they found can seriously reduce power. The resampled differences were centred on the observed difference, and p was the share of them lying at least as far from it as the observed difference lies from zero. It was corrected for false discovery rate within the eight metrics of one contrast at one station.

Daily fire occurrence has been modelled statistically since Bruce (1960), whose negative binomial model related daily counts to a fire danger rating index and which @taylor2013prediction identified as the first stochastic model of fire occurrence. Canadian operational practice later moved to logistic models of fire presence, because, as @taylor2013prediction noted, "overdispersion is of concern when Poisson-based methods are used to model counts" [@taylor2013prediction, p. 591]. @martell1987logistic predicted the probability of a people-caused fire day in northern Ontario by logistic regression with a Poisson assumption for the daily count, and @martell1989seasonal added periodic functions of the calendar day to represent seasonal variation. Count models remain in use where the daily number is the quantity of interest. @plucinski2014bushfires modelled daily human-caused bushfires in south-west Western Australia by negative binomial regression on fuel moisture, fitted on three years and tested on an independent fourth, and @xiao2015count found that a negative binomial mixed model described forest fire counts in Guizhou, China, better than Poisson, zero-inflated and hurdle alternatives. The closest regional precedent is @magnussen2012bc, who modelled daily lightning- and human-caused fire occurrence across British Columbia from 1981 to 2000 by logistic regression on lightning strikes, forest cover, surface weather, atmospheric stability and Fire Weather Index System moisture codes, and under leave-one-year-out cross-validation predicted the daily provincial number of lightning fires at R = 0.83 and of human-caused fires at R = 0.55 [@magnussen2012bc].

Daily ignition counts here were modelled by negative binomial regression with a log link [@lawless1987negbin], because the response was a daily basin count rather than a cell-day presence. The linear predictor carried the daily basin danger value, two annual harmonics in day of year in the manner of @martell1989seasonal, season as a factor, and the number of stations that contributed to the basin mean that day, since no station reports in every season and the composition of the network changes. That last term cannot affect the comparison between series in any case, because all three are averaged over exactly the same stations on exactly the same days. The seasonal terms matter beyond this study, since @castelclavera2025comparative found in Mediterranean France that "relying solely on fire-weather indices is insufficient for efficient rating of fire activities" and that spatial and seasonal effects were needed, even though the Canadian Fire Weather Index was the most skilful index they tested. The lightning model carried no strike term, because no strike record covered the window, and lightning occurrence models depend on one. @flannigan1991lightning explained nearly 50 per cent of the variance in daily lightning fire counts in northwestern Ontario with the Duff Moisture Code and the multiplicity of negative discharges, @wotton2005lightning found that a sheltered duff moisture index was the strongest predictor of ignition given a strike, and @wierzchowski2002lightning recorded one fire for every 50 lightning discharges in British Columbia against one for every 1,400 in Alberta. The Canadian Lightning Detection Network climatology of @kochtubajda2020cldn covers 1999 to 2018, so it misses the first `r 1999 - yr_first` seasons of this window and the last `r yr_last - 2018`.

Predictive skill was compared by leaving one season out at a time, refitting without it, and scoring the held-out season, which is the blocked cross-validation @roberts2017crossvalidation recommend for temporally structured data, since random splits of such data result "in serious underestimation of predictive error" [@roberts2017crossvalidation], and the leave-one-year-out design @magnussen2012bc used for British Columbia. Each held-out season was scored by its log likelihood under the refitted model, the logarithmic score that @gneiting2007scoring showed to be strictly proper. They also noted that scores for competing forecasts "are directly comparable if they refer to exactly the same set of forecast situations" [@gneiting2007scoring, p. 362], which held here because the three series were scored on the same days. Series were compared on held-out likelihood rather than on in-sample fit because three series computed from one weather record will all fit, and the question is which predicts. One caution from the index comparison literature applies directly. @eastaugh2012cautionary compared four hypothetical indices, three of them simple transformations of one another, and found that all the established comparators they examined except the c-index "indicate different predictive power between the effectively identical indices", the differences "resulting from the frequency distributions of the index values rather than from any real difference in predictive power" [@eastaugh2012cautionary, p. 932]. The three series here are close to transformations of one another, and a log-linear danger term is sensitive to the shape of their distributions, so a small likelihood difference between them is not evidence of a difference in predictive power.

What a window of `r n_seasons` seasons cannot resolve was computed rather than hedged, following @weatherhead1998detection, who showed that the number of years needed to detect a trend grows with the variance and the lag-one autocorrelation of the noise, from about 10 to more than 20 years for a trend of 5 per cent per decade, and that a level shift from a change of instrument or site can raise that number by 50 per cent or more. @tiao1990autocorrelation had shown that the precision of a trend estimate depends critically on autocorrelation and on record length, and @wang2020power showed by simulation that the power of the Mann-Kendall test rises with slope and record length, falls with variance, and that positive autocorrelation increases both the Type I and the Type II error. For each metric the minimum detectable trend was the slope at which a two-sided test at alpha 0.05 would reach 80 per cent power given the residual spread of that metric about its own Theil-Sen line, adjusted for the lower efficiency of the Theil-Sen estimator under normal errors and inflated for serial correlation by the factor that @weatherhead1998detection derived for first-order autoregressive noise, the square root of (1 + phi) / (1 - phi), where phi is the lag-one autocorrelation of the residuals in season order. Phi was bounded between 0 and 0.9, so that a negative sample estimate could not make the detectable trend smaller than it would be for independent seasons.
