The extreme-day counts are counts of rare days, and @frei2001rare found that in a 100-year record a 1.5-fold change in the frequency of an event was detected with probability 0.6 when the event had an average return period of 30 days but only 0.2 at a return period of 100 days, so the least frequent thresholds were expected to be the least detectable. A null result was reported against the minimum detectable trend, so that "no trend detected" was kept separate from "no trend".


# Results {#sec-results}

```{r}
#| label: load-results
#| echo: true
#| output: false
series_daily <- read.csv(file.path(derived, "fwi-series-daily.csv"),
                         stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
series_daily$date <- as.Date(series_daily$date)
metrics <- read.csv(file.path(derived, "seasonal-metrics.csv"),
                    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
thresh_pct <- read.csv(file.path(derived, "threshold-percentiles.csv"),
                       stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
basin <- read.csv(file.path(derived, "basin-daily.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
basin$date <- as.Date(basin$date)

# Relative-threshold counts are replaced by the in-base bootstrap estimates of
# Zhang et al. (2005), computed from the same daily series and the same
# 1991 to 2020 base period. Out-of-base seasons are unchanged by construction;
# the check below stops the render if any is not.
corrected <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(SERIES), function(s)
  inbase_corrected_counts(series_daily, s, probs = c(90, 95),
                          reference = c(1991, 2020))))
for (pp in c(90, 95)) {
  col <- paste0("n_fwi_p", pp)
  cc <- corrected[corrected$prob == pp, c("station_name", "series", "year", "count")]
  key_m <- paste(metrics$station_name, metrics$series, metrics$year)
  key_c <- paste(cc$station_name, cc$series, cc$year)
  new <- cc$count[match(key_m, key_c)]
  out_base <- metrics$year > 2020 & is.finite(metrics[[col]])
  if (any(abs(new[out_base] - metrics[[col]][out_base]) > 1e-9))
    stop("in-base correction changed an out-of-base count for ", col)
  metrics[[paste0(col, "_uncorrected")]] <- metrics[[col]]
  metrics[[col]] <- new
}
```

## Implementation Checks

```{r}
#| label: tbl-verify
#| tbl-cap: "Verification of the FWI1987 implementation. The first block compares it against the CRAN package cffdrs over the Petawawa Research Forest test record. The second compares it against the FWI1987 codes BC Wildfire Service computed operationally at these stations, pooled over all kept station-seasons."
#| echo: true
val <- read.csv(file.path(derived, "fwi1987-validation.csv"),
                stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
opc <- read.csv(file.path(derived, "fwi1987-operational-check.csv"),
                stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# The two blocks differ by ten orders of magnitude, so the differences are
# formatted as strings rather than left to the table's numeric printing, which
# would render machine epsilon as a wall of zeros.
fmt_diff <- function(x) ifelse(is.na(x), "", formatC(x, format = "g", digits = 3))

blk1 <- data.frame(
  Check = "against cffdrs",
  Component = val$component,
  n = format(val$n, big.mark = ","),
  `Max absolute difference` = fmt_diff(val$max_abs_diff),
  `Mean absolute difference` = fmt_diff(val$mean_abs_diff),
  `Correlation` = "",
  check.names = FALSE)

# The data mart names the operational columns in full; the initials are the
# component names used everywhere else in this document.
initials <- function(x) vapply(strsplit(x, "_"),
                               function(p) paste0(substr(p, 1, 1), collapse = ""),
                               character(1))
op_agg <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(opc, opc$component), function(d) {
  data.frame(
    Check = "against operational codes",
    Component = initials(d$component[1]),
    n = format(sum(d$n), big.mark = ","),
    `Max absolute difference` = "",
    `Mean absolute difference` = fmt_diff(weighted.mean(abs(d$mean_bias), d$n)),
    `Correlation` = formatC(weighted.mean(d$pearson_r, d$n), format = "f", digits = 4),
    check.names = FALSE)
}))
rownames(op_agg) <- NULL
fmt_tbl(rbind(blk1, op_agg))
```

```{r}
#| label: verify-prose
#| echo: true
#| output: false
max_cffdrs <- max(val$max_abs_diff)
op_r <- weighted.mean(opc$pearson_r, opc$n)
op_n <- sum(opc$n)
bias_of <- function(comp) {
  d <- opc[opc$component == comp, ]
  weighted.mean(abs(d$mean_bias), d$n)
}
r_of <- function(comp) {
  d <- opc[opc$component == comp, ]
  weighted.mean(d$pearson_r, d$n)
}
dc_bias <- bias_of("DROUGHT_CODE")
bui_bias <- bias_of("BUILDUP_INDEX")
ffmc_r <- r_of("FINE_FUEL_MOISTURE_CODE")
```

@tbl-verify gives both checks. Against `cffdrs` the two implementations agreed to `r formatC(max_cffdrs, format = "g", digits = 2)` across all seven components, which is machine precision, because they are the same arithmetic, and the check confirmed that the equations were transcribed correctly rather than that they are correct.

Against the operational codes, computed by a different party in a different decade, the weighted mean correlation over `r n_fmt(op_n)` station-days was `r round(op_r, 3)`. That check was not expected to be exact, and one of its disagreements was large and had a known cause. The mean absolute bias in the Drought Code was `r round(dc_bias, 0)` units, and in the Buildup Index, which is computed from it, `r round(bui_bias, 1)`. BC Wildfire Service overwinters the Drought Code, carrying it from the previous autumn, whereas this study restarted it at 15 on 1 April, because these stations report no winter weather for an overwintering calculation to use. That is a difference in convention, not an error, and its direction is known, in that a restarted Drought Code is lower than an overwintered one. Every absolute Drought Code and Buildup Index level reported here is conditional on that convention, and it cannot affect any comparison between the three series, because all three restart identically.

The components that do not depend on the overwintered code agreed closely. The Fine Fuel Moisture Code correlated `r round(opc$pearson_r[opc$component == "FINE_FUEL_MOISTURE_CODE"] |> weighted.mean(opc$n[opc$component == "FINE_FUEL_MOISTURE_CODE"]), 4)` with the operational value, which is the component the version comparison principally rests on.

## Threshold Positions

```{r}
#| label: tbl-thresholds
#| tbl-cap: "Where each absolute threshold falls in each series' own 1991 to 2020 reference distribution, averaged over stations. A threshold at the same percentile in every series would mean the three systems are interchangeable for counting extremes. The reference median is the median of that component over the same distribution."
#| echo: true
tp <- do.call(rbind, lapply(
  split(thresh_pct, list(thresh_pct$series, thresh_pct$component,
                         thresh_pct$threshold), drop = TRUE),
  function(d) data.frame(
    Series = unname(SERIES[d$series[1]]),
    Component = toupper(d$component[1]),
    Threshold = d$threshold[1],
    `Percentile of threshold` = round(mean(d$percentile_of_threshold, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    `Days per season above` = NA_real_,
    `Reference median` = round(mean(d$reference_median, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    check.names = FALSE)))
# Days per season above each absolute threshold, averaged over station-seasons.
days_above <- function(series, component, thr) {
  col <- switch(paste(component, thr),
                "ffmc 91" = "n_ffmc_ge91",
                "fwi 19" = "n_fwi_ge19",
                "fwi 30" = "n_fwi_ge30")
  mean(metrics[[col]][metrics$series == series], na.rm = TRUE)
}
key <- do.call(rbind, strsplit(rownames(tp), "\\."))
tp$`Days per season above` <- round(mapply(days_above, key[, 1], key[, 2],
                                           as.numeric(key[, 3])), 1)
tp <- tp[order(tp$Component, tp$Threshold, tp$Series), ]
rownames(tp) <- NULL
fmt_tbl(tp)
```

```{r}
#| label: threshold-prose
#| echo: true
#| output: false
ffmc91 <- subset(tp, Component == "FFMC" & Threshold == 91)
fwi19 <- subset(tp, Component == "FWI" & Threshold == 19)
p_s1 <- ffmc91$`Percentile of threshold`[grepl("S1", ffmc91$Series)]
p_s2 <- ffmc91$`Percentile of threshold`[grepl("S2", ffmc91$Series)]
p_s3 <- ffmc91$`Percentile of threshold`[grepl("S3", ffmc91$Series)]
d_s1 <- ffmc91$`Days per season above`[grepl("S1", ffmc91$Series)]
d_s2 <- ffmc91$`Days per season above`[grepl("S2", ffmc91$Series)]
d_s3 <- ffmc91$`Days per season above`[grepl("S3", ffmc91$Series)]
```

@tbl-thresholds tests the comparability sentence of @cffdg2025fwi2025 directly. A Fine Fuel Moisture Code of 91 sat at the `r p_s1`th percentile of the S1 distribution, the `r p_s2`th of S2 and the `r p_s3`th of S3, which in days per season above it was `r d_s1` under S1, `r d_s2` under S2 and `r d_s3` under S3.

```{r}
#| label: threshold-reading
#| echo: true
#| output: false
# The comparability claim is about where a value sits, so the reading is stated
# in the two units that matter and neither is rounded away: the percentile spread
# across series, and the difference in days per season an agency would count.
pct_spread <- max(abs(p_s3 - p_s1), abs(p_s2 - p_s1))
day_gap <- d_s3 - d_s1
day_gap_pct <- 100 * day_gap / d_s1
```

The claim survived as a statement about levels and did not survive as a statement about counts. The three medians of the Fine Fuel Moisture Code over the reference period sat within about a unit of each other, so a value of 91 does mean much what it used to mean, but the same threshold selected `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(day_gap))` `r if (day_gap >= 0) "more" else "fewer"` days per season under S3 than under S1, a difference of `r sprintf("%.0f", abs(day_gap_pct))` per cent, because the percentile it occupied moved by `r sprintf("%.1f", pct_spread)` points. Those are the same distributions, described two ways, and @fig-distributions shows why, in that the curves sit almost on top of one another through the middle and separate where the threshold is.

```{r}
#| label: fig-distributions
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-dpi: 300
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of the daily Fine Fuel Moisture Code and the daily Fire Weather Index over all kept station-days under the three series, with the absolute thresholds marked. The comparability claim of the 2025 report concerns the position of a value on the scale; an extreme-day count concerns the mass beyond a threshold, which is a different quantity."
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 1.4, 1), mgp = c(2.4, 0.7, 0), cex = 0.75)
cols <- c(s1 = "#1B4F72", s2 = "#B7950B", s3 = "#943126")

plot_dens <- function(cols_prefix, xlab, cuts, xlim) {
  dens <- lapply(names(cols), function(s) {
    v <- series_daily[[paste0(s, "_", cols_prefix)]]
    density(v[is.finite(v)], na.rm = TRUE)
  })
  ymax <- max(vapply(dens, function(d) max(d$y), numeric(1)))
  plot(NA, xlim = xlim, ylim = c(0, ymax * 1.05), xlab = xlab,
       ylab = "Density", main = "")
  for (i in seq_along(dens)) lines(dens[[i]], col = cols[i], lwd = 1.8)
  abline(v = cuts, lty = 3, col = "grey30")
  legend("topleft", legend = unname(SERIES), col = cols, lwd = 1.8, bty = "n",
         cex = 0.72)
}
plot_dens("ffmc", "Fine Fuel Moisture Code", 91, c(40, 101))
plot_dens("fwi", "Fire Weather Index", c(19, 30), c(0, 60))
par(op)
```

## Mechanism

```{r}
#| label: fig-mechanism
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| fig-dpi: 300
#| fig-cap: "Ten days of the hourly Fine Fuel Moisture Code at Penticton RS in August 2003, under FWI2025 driven by the observed hourly weather and under FWI2025 driven by the 13:00 observation alone. Both are the same system on the same days, and the only difference is the weather input the System received. The vertical lines mark 13:00 local daylight time, the hour FWI1987 observes, and 17:00, the hour a daily value conventionally represents."
ex <- read.csv(file.path(derived, "example-season-hourly.csv"),
               stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
ex$t <- as.POSIXct(sprintf("%04d-%02d-%02d %02d:00:00", ex$yr, ex$mon, ex$day, ex$hr),
                   tz = "UTC")
win <- ex[ex$mon == 8 & ex$day >= 14 & ex$day <= 23, ]

op <- par(mar = c(3.2, 4, 1.2, 1), cex = 0.8)
plot(win$t, win$s3_ffmc, type = "l", col = cols["s3"], lwd = 1.6,
     ylim = range(c(win$s3_ffmc, win$s2_ffmc), na.rm = TRUE),
     xlab = "", ylab = "Fine Fuel Moisture Code", xaxt = "n")
lines(win$t, win$s2_ffmc, col = cols["s2"], lwd = 1.6)
axis.POSIXct(1, win$t, format = "%d %b")
# The hour markers are drawn thin and pale on purpose: they locate the two
# sampling hours without competing with the curves, which are the subject.
abline(v = win$t[win$hr == 12], col = "grey86", lty = 3, lwd = 0.6)
abline(v = win$t[win$hr == 16], col = "grey62", lty = 2, lwd = 0.6)
lines(win$t, win$s3_ffmc, col = cols["s3"], lwd = 1.6)
lines(win$t, win$s2_ffmc, col = cols["s2"], lwd = 1.6)
legend("bottomleft", bty = "n", cex = 0.75,
       legend = c(unname(SERIES[c("s3", "s2")]),
                  "13:00 LDT, the FWI1987 observation", "17:00 LDT"),
       col = c(cols["s3"], cols["s2"], "grey86", "grey62"),
       lwd = c(1.6, 1.6, 0.8, 0.8), lty = c(1, 1, 3, 2))
par(op)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-capability
#| tbl-cap: "Two quantities FWI2025 reports and FWI1987 cannot, the hour at which peak burning conditions occur and the number of hours per day the burning window stays open, both as the specification's own daily summary computes them. Values are means over kept station-seasons. FWI1987 has no entry because a system with one value per day cannot say when in the day it applies."
#| echo: true
cap <- metrics[metrics$series %in% c("s2", "s3") &
                 !is.na(metrics$mean_peak_hr), ]
if (nrow(cap)) {
  ct <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(cap, cap$series), function(d) data.frame(
    Series = unname(SERIES[d$series[1]]),
    `Mean peak hour (LST)` = round(mean(d$mean_peak_hr, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    `Mean burning window (h)` = round(mean(d$mean_duration, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    `Days per season with window >= 6 h` = round(mean(d$n_duration_ge6, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    check.names = FALSE)))
  rownames(ct) <- NULL
  fmt_tbl(ct)
} else {
  stop("seasonal-metrics.csv carries no daily summary columns; re-run build_seasonal_metrics.py")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: mechanism-reading
#| echo: true
#| output: false
# The two readings the figure supports, computed from the same window it draws.
night <- win$hr %in% c(2, 3, 4, 5)
day <- win$hr %in% c(14, 15, 16, 17)
night_gap <- mean(win$s3_ffmc[night] - win$s2_ffmc[night], na.rm = TRUE)
day_gap <- mean(win$s3_ffmc[day] - win$s2_ffmc[day], na.rm = TRUE)
range_s3 <- mean(tapply(win$s3_ffmc, win$day, function(v) diff(range(v))))
range_s2 <- mean(tapply(win$s2_ffmc, win$day, function(v) diff(range(v))))
```

@fig-mechanism shows what separated S2 from S3 on the same ten days. Both are FWI2025, both were given the same rain, and the only difference was whether the System received the observed hourly weather or reconstructed a standard diurnal curve from the 13:00 observation.

The reconstruction was not a smoothed version of the observation but a different shape. Over these days it swung `r sprintf("%.1f", range_s2)` code units between its daily minimum and maximum against `r sprintf("%.1f", range_s3)` for the observed series, and the difference was concentrated overnight, in that the two ran `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(day_gap))` units apart in the mid-afternoon and `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(night_gap))` units apart before dawn. A standard curve anchored to one afternoon reading estimates the night, and it estimated it wetter than the nights actually were. @tbl-capability gives the consequence in the two quantities only the hourly system produces at all.

## Trends

```{r}
#| label: trend-compute
#| echo: true
#| output: false
# The metric family. Each entry is a column of the seasonal metric table, a
# label, and which thresholding scheme it belongs to. The family is declared
# here, once, and the false discovery rate correction is applied within it.
METRICS <- data.frame(
  col = c("mean_fwi", "ssr", "peak_bui",
          "n_ffmc_ge91", "n_fwi_ge19", "n_fwi_ge30",
          "n_fwi_p90", "n_fwi_p95"),
  label = c("Mean FWI", "Seasonal severity rating", "Peak BUI",
            "Days FFMC >= 91", "Days FWI >= 19", "Days FWI >= 30",
            "Days above own 90th percentile", "Days above own 95th percentile"),
  scheme = c("level", "level", "level",
             "absolute", "absolute", "absolute",
             "relative", "relative"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# Trends are estimated per station and per series, then combined, rather than on
# a basin average, because the set of reporting stations changes between seasons
# and a basin average would move when a station joins or leaves.
trend_rows <- list()
for (s in names(SERIES)) {
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(METRICS))) {
    m <- METRICS$col[i]
    for (stn in unique(metrics$station_name)) {
      d <- metrics[metrics$series == s & metrics$station_name == stn, ]
      d <- d[is.finite(d[[m]]), ]
      if (nrow(d) < 15) next
      tt <- trend_test(d$year, d[[m]])
      tt$series <- s; tt$metric <- m; tt$station <- stn
      tt$mdt <- minimum_detectable_trend(d$year, d[[m]])
      trend_rows[[length(trend_rows) + 1]] <- tt
    }
  }
}
trends <- do.call(rbind, trend_rows)
if (is.null(trends) || !nrow(trends))
  stop("No station has the 15 seasons the trend estimator requires. ",
       "Kept station-seasons: ", n_kept, " over ", n_seasons, " seasons. ",
       "Re-run 05.scripts/fetch_fire_weather.py and ",
       "05.scripts/compute_fwi_series.py over the full archive.")
# The family is the eight metrics within one series at one station.
trends$q <- ave(trends$p_corrected,
                paste(trends$series, trends$station), FUN = fdr)
write.csv(trends, file.path(outputs, "trend-estimates.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-trends
#| tbl-cap: "Theil-Sen slopes per season for each seasonal metric under each series, pooled across stations as the median station slope, with the range across stations. Significance is Mann-Kendall with the Hamed and Rao variance correction; the count is of stations at which the false discovery rate adjusted p value falls below 0.05 within that station's eight-metric family. The minimum detectable trend is the slope this record could resolve at 80 per cent power."
#| echo: true
tr <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(trends, list(trends$series, trends$metric),
                                  drop = TRUE), function(d) {
  data.frame(
    Series = unname(SERIES[d$series[1]]),
    Metric = METRICS$label[match(d$metric[1], METRICS$col)],
    Stations = nrow(d),
    `Median slope` = round(median(d$slope, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    `Slope range` = sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", min(d$slope, na.rm = TRUE),
                            max(d$slope, na.rm = TRUE)),
    `Stations q < 0.05` = sum(d$q < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Min detectable` = round(median(d$mdt, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    check.names = FALSE)
}))
tr <- tr[order(match(tr$Metric, METRICS$label), tr$Series), ]
rownames(tr) <- NULL
fmt_tbl(tr)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-trends
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 7.0
#| fig-dpi: 300
#| fig-cap: "Seasonal metrics by season under the three series, pooled across stations as the station mean, with the Theil-Sen line for each series. The absolute and relative extreme-day counts are the panels the second question turned on, under the prediction that the absolute counts separate between series and the relative counts do not."
show <- c("mean_fwi", "ssr", "n_ffmc_ge91", "n_fwi_ge19", "n_fwi_p90", "n_fwi_p95")
# Generous bottom margin and tightened axis title placement: at three rows on one
# page the default margin clips the x axis label against the panel below.
op <- par(mfrow = c(3, 2), mar = c(3.8, 4, 1.4, 1), mgp = c(2.4, 0.7, 0),
          cex = 0.68)
for (m in show) {
  ylab <- METRICS$label[match(m, METRICS$col)]
  rng <- range(metrics[[m]], na.rm = TRUE)
  plot(NA, xlim = range(metrics$year), ylim = rng, xlab = "Season", ylab = ylab,
       main = "")
  for (s in names(SERIES)) {
    d <- metrics[metrics$series == s, ]
    a <- aggregate(d[[m]], list(year = d$year), mean, na.rm = TRUE)
    points(a$year, a$x, col = cols[s], pch = 16, cex = 0.6)
    sl <- theil_sen(a$year, a$x)
    ic <- median(a$x - sl * a$year)
    abline(a = ic, b = sl, col = cols[s], lwd = 1.6)
  }
  if (m == show[1])
    legend("topleft", legend = unname(SERIES), col = cols, lwd = 1.6, bty = "n",
           cex = 0.7)
}
par(op)
```

```{r}
#| label: trend-reading
#| echo: true
#| output: false
# The direction and strength of the trend picture, computed rather than eyeballed
# off the table, so the sentence below cannot say something the numbers do not.
tr_up <- sum(trends$slope > 0, na.rm = TRUE)
tr_n <- sum(is.finite(trends$slope))
tr_sig <- sum(trends$q < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
tr_sig_up <- sum(trends$q < 0.05 & trends$slope > 0, na.rm = TRUE)
# What the autocorrelation correction cost, in tests that would otherwise pass.
would_pass <- sum(p.adjust(trends$p_uncorrected, "BH") < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
infl <- median(trends$n_over_nstar, na.rm = TRUE)
# The two extremes among the extreme-day counts, which share the unit days per
# season, so that the paragraph names its highest and lowest cases rather than
# reporting only a count of how many passed.
day_tr <- trends[trends$metric %in% METRICS$col[METRICS$scheme != "level"], ]
hi <- day_tr[which.max(day_tr$slope), ]
lo <- day_tr[which.min(day_tr$slope), ]
name_case <- function(r) sprintf("%s under %s at %s (%+.2f days per season, q = %s)",
  METRICS$label[match(r$metric, METRICS$col)], unname(SERIES_PROSE[r$series]),
  station_prose(r$station),
  r$slope, ifelse(r$q < 0.001, "< 0.001", sprintf("%.3f", r$q)))
```

Of the `r tr_n` station, series and metric combinations in @tbl-trends, `r tr_up` had a positive Theil-Sen slope. After the Hamed and Rao correction for serial correlation and the false discovery rate correction within each station's eight-metric family, `r tr_sig` remained below a q value of 0.05, `r tr_sig_up` of them positive. The serial correlation correction mattered, because the median ratio of nominal to effective sample size was `r sprintf("%.2f", infl)`, and `r would_pass` combinations would have passed the same false discovery threshold had the uncorrected variance been used. Among the extreme-day counts, which share the unit days per season, the steepest rise was in `r name_case(hi)` and the `r if (lo$slope < 0) "steepest fall" else "shallowest rise"` in `r name_case(lo)`.

Two cautions belong with that count. The number of stations with enough seasons to carry a trend was `r length(unique(trends$station))`, because a station needed 15 usable seasons and this network did not give many of them, and for most metrics the observed change over the window was smaller than the change this record could have resolved, which is set out quantitatively in @sec-discussion. A trend estimate here is a direction with a wide interval, not a measurement.

@fig-trends puts the three series side by side. The panels that bear on the second question are the two absolute-threshold counts against the two relative-threshold counts, because that contrast, and not the overall direction, is what the second question turned on.

## Version Dependence

```{r}
#| label: slopediff-compute
#| echo: true
#| output: false
CONTRASTS <- list(
  c("s1", "s2", "Version change, input held at 13:00"),
  c("s2", "s3", "Input resolution change, version held at FWI2025"),
  c("s1", "s3", "Operational migration, both changes")
)

diff_rows <- list()
for (cn in CONTRASTS) {
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(METRICS))) {
    m <- METRICS$col[i]
    for (stn in unique(metrics$station_name)) {
      a <- metrics[metrics$series == cn[1] & metrics$station_name == stn,
                   c("year", m)]
      b <- metrics[metrics$series == cn[2] & metrics$station_name == stn,
                   c("year", m)]
      w <- merge(a, b, by = "year", suffixes = c(".a", ".b"))
      names(w)[2:3] <- c("a", "b")
      if (nrow(w) < 15) next
      sd_ <- slope_difference(w)
      sd_$contrast <- cn[3]; sd_$metric <- m; sd_$station <- stn
      sd_$scheme <- METRICS$scheme[i]
      diff_rows[[length(diff_rows) + 1]] <- sd_
    }
  }
}
sdiff <- do.call(rbind, diff_rows)
if (is.null(sdiff) || !nrow(sdiff))
  stop("No station-series pair has the 15 paired seasons the bootstrap requires.")
# The family here is the eight metrics within one contrast at one station: one
# station's answer to one of the three questions the design asks.
sdiff$q <- ave(sdiff$p_two_sided, paste(sdiff$contrast, sdiff$station), FUN = fdr)
write.csv(sdiff, file.path(outputs, "slope-differences.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-slopediff
#| tbl-cap: "Difference in Theil-Sen slope between series, by metric and contrast, pooled across stations as the median. Intervals are paired moving-block bootstrap percentile intervals over 4,000 resamples of blocks of consecutive seasons, which preserves both the dependence between series that share a weather record and the serial correlation within each. Stations excluding zero counts the stations whose own interval does not contain zero; the last column applies the Benjamini and Hochberg correction within each station's eight-metric family for that contrast."
#| echo: true
sd_tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(
  split(sdiff, list(sdiff$contrast, sdiff$metric), drop = TRUE), function(d) {
    data.frame(
      Contrast = d$contrast[1],
      Scheme = d$scheme[1],
      Metric = METRICS$label[match(d$metric[1], METRICS$col)],
      Stations = nrow(d),
      `Median difference` = round(median(d$difference, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
      `Stations excluding zero` = sum(d$lower > 0 | d$upper < 0, na.rm = TRUE),
      `Stations q < 0.05` = sum(d$q < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
      check.names = FALSE)
  }))
sd_tab <- sd_tab[order(match(sd_tab$Contrast, vapply(CONTRASTS, `[`, "", 3)),
                       match(sd_tab$Metric, METRICS$label)), ]
rownames(sd_tab) <- NULL
fmt_tbl(sd_tab)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-slopediff
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-dpi: 300
#| fig-cap: "Difference in Theil-Sen slope between series for the five extreme-day counts, which all measure days per season and therefore share one axis. Points are station estimates, bars are paired moving-block bootstrap 95 per cent intervals over 4,000 resamples of blocks of consecutive seasons. Red marks the three absolute thresholds and blue the two thresholds internal to each series. The prediction under test is that the red points separate from zero and the blue ones do not. The three level metrics are omitted from this figure because the seasonal severity rating is measured on a scale two orders of magnitude larger and would compress everything else to a point; they are in the preceding table."
# Only the metrics measured in days per season are drawn, so one x axis means the
# same thing everywhere on the figure. A common range across the three panels
# keeps the contrasts comparable, and the labels are drawn once on the left.
DAY_METRICS <- METRICS$col[METRICS$scheme %in% c("absolute", "relative")]
sd_plot <- sdiff[sdiff$metric %in% DAY_METRICS, ]
sd_plot$mi <- match(sd_plot$metric, METRICS$col)
xr <- range(c(sd_plot$lower, sd_plot$upper, 0), na.rm = TRUE)

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), oma = c(0, 12.5, 0, 0), mgp = c(2.2, 0.6, 0), cex = 0.62)
for (k in seq_along(CONTRASTS)) {
  cn <- CONTRASTS[[k]]
  d <- sd_plot[sd_plot$contrast == cn[3], ]
  par(mar = c(4, 0.6, 3.4, 0.6))
  if (!nrow(d)) { plot.new(); next }
  d <- d[order(d$mi, d$station), ]
  y <- seq_len(nrow(d))
  plot(NA, xlim = xr, ylim = c(0.5, max(y) + 0.5), yaxt = "n",
       xlab = "Slope difference, days per season", ylab = "",
       main = paste(strwrap(cn[3], 24), collapse = "\n"), cex.main = 0.95)
  abline(v = 0, col = "grey50", lty = 2)
  segments(d$lower, y, d$upper, y, col = "grey35")
  points(d$difference, y, pch = 16, cex = 0.8,
         col = ifelse(d$scheme == "absolute", "#943126", "#1B4F72"))
  if (k == 1)
    axis(2, at = y, labels = paste0(METRICS$label[d$mi], ", ", d$station),
         las = 1, cex.axis = 0.7, tick = FALSE, line = -0.3, outer = TRUE)
}
par(op)
```

```{r}
#| label: slopediff-reading
#| echo: true
#| output: false
# The hypothesis has a specific shape: absolute-threshold counts should separate
# between series and relative-threshold counts should not. That shape is scored
# here as two rates, so the sentence below reports what the numbers show rather
# than what the hypothesis predicted.
score <- function(contrast, scheme) {
  d <- sdiff[sdiff$contrast == contrast & sdiff$scheme == scheme, ]
  if (!nrow(d)) return(c(n = 0, sig = 0, rate = NA_real_, med = NA_real_))
  sig <- sum(d$q < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
  c(n = nrow(d), sig = sig, rate = 100 * sig / nrow(d),
    med = median(d$difference, na.rm = TRUE))
}
ver_label <- CONTRASTS[[1]][3]
inp_label <- CONTRASTS[[2]][3]
mig_label <- CONTRASTS[[3]][3]
sc <- rbind(
  `version, absolute`   = score(ver_label, "absolute"),
  `version, relative`   = score(ver_label, "relative"),
  `input, absolute`     = score(inp_label, "absolute"),
  `input, relative`     = score(inp_label, "relative"),
  `migration, absolute` = score(mig_label, "absolute"),
  `migration, relative` = score(mig_label, "relative"))
sc <- as.data.frame(sc)
write.csv(sc, file.path(outputs, "hypothesis-scoring.csv"))

# The resolution of the difference test, so that a null is readable. The half
# width of the bootstrap interval is the smallest difference this record could
# have separated from zero at each station and metric.
sdiff$halfwidth <- (sdiff$upper - sdiff$lower) / 2
res_abs <- median(sdiff$halfwidth[sdiff$scheme == "absolute"], na.rm = TRUE)
res_rel <- median(sdiff$halfwidth[sdiff$scheme == "relative"], na.rm = TRUE)
n_any_sig <- sum(sdiff$q < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)

verdict <- if (!is.finite(sc["migration, absolute", "rate"])) {
  "could not be scored"
} else if (sc["migration, absolute", "rate"] > sc["migration, relative", "rate"]) {
  "in the direction the mechanism predicts"
} else if (sc["migration, absolute", "rate"] < sc["migration, relative", "rate"]) {
  "in the opposite direction to the one the mechanism predicts"
} else {
  "with no difference between the two thresholding schemes"
}
```

@tbl-slopediff and @fig-slopediff decompose the difference. The prediction under test was that absolute-threshold counts would separate between series while relative-threshold counts would not, because the version change was expected to widen the tail without moving the level. Scored on the migration contrast, the one an agency faces, the absolute-threshold metrics gave a difference excluding zero at `r sprintf("%.0f", sc["migration, absolute", "rate"])` per cent of station-metric combinations against `r sprintf("%.0f", sc["migration, relative", "rate"])` per cent for the relative-threshold metrics. That was `r verdict`.

Where the rates were zero the statement is about resolution and not about the System. Across all `r nrow(sdiff)` station, metric and contrast combinations, `r n_any_sig` gave a slope difference whose corrected interval excluded zero. The median half width of those intervals was `r sprintf("%.3f", res_abs)` days per season for the absolute-threshold metrics and `r sprintf("%.3f", res_rel)` for the relative ones, which over the `r yr_last - yr_first` season window is `r sprintf("%.1f", res_abs * (yr_last - yr_first))` and `r sprintf("%.1f", res_rel * (yr_last - yr_first))` days respectively. A difference in trend smaller than that would not have been separated from zero here, and the level differences reported above were considerably larger than the trend differences, which is the substantive point, because the version change moved where the distribution sits far more than it moved how fast it is moving.

Splitting the migration into its two halves, the version change alone gave `r sprintf("%.0f", sc["version, absolute", "rate"])` per cent of absolute-metric differences excluding zero and the input resolution change alone gave `r sprintf("%.0f", sc["input, absolute", "rate"])` per cent. The median differences are `r sprintf("%.3f", sc["version, absolute", "med"])` and `r sprintf("%.3f", sc["input, absolute", "med"])` per season respectively, against `r sprintf("%.3f", sc["migration, absolute", "med"])` for the two together, which is the additivity the design predicted if the two changes do not interact.

## Summary Hour Sensitivity

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sensitivity
#| tbl-cap: "Sensitivity of the absolute extreme-day counts to how an hourly series is reduced to a daily value. The fixed hour is 16:00 Local Standard Time, 17:00 local daylight time. The daily maximum takes the largest of the 24 hourly values, which must be at least as large and is reported only to bound the effect of the choice. FWI1987 produces one value per day and so appears once."
#| echo: true
sens_cols <- c("n_ffmc_ge91", "n_ffmc_max_ge91", "n_fwi_ge19", "n_fwi_max_ge19")
have <- sens_cols %in% names(metrics)
if (all(have)) {
  sens <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(metrics, metrics$series), function(d) data.frame(
    Series = unname(SERIES[d$series[1]]),
    `Days FFMC >= 91, fixed hour` = round(mean(d$n_ffmc_ge91, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    `Days FFMC >= 91, daily maximum` = round(mean(d$n_ffmc_max_ge91, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    `Days FWI >= 19, fixed hour` = round(mean(d$n_fwi_ge19, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    `Days FWI >= 19, daily maximum` = round(mean(d$n_fwi_max_ge19, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    check.names = FALSE)))
  rownames(sens) <- NULL
  fmt_tbl(sens)
} else {
  stop("seasonal-metrics.csv carries no daily maximum columns; re-run build_seasonal_metrics.py")
}
```

@tbl-sensitivity bounds the effect of the summary rule. Taking the daily maximum of 24 hourly values instead of one fixed hour raised every count in the two FWI2025 series and could not lower any of them, which is why it was not the primary, since part of that rise is the order statistic and not the System.

## Ignition Skill

```{r}
#| label: ignition-compute
#| echo: true
#| output: false
mod_dat <- merge(basin, ign_daily, by = c("date", "year", "doy"))
mod_dat <- mod_dat[format(mod_dat$date, "%m") %in% c("05", "06", "07", "08", "09"), ]

SKILL_RESPONSES <- c("n_lightning_all", "n_total_all")

RESPONSES <- c(n_lightning_all = "Lightning, no size limit",
               n_person_all = "Person, no size limit",
               n_total_all = "All causes, no size limit",
               n_total_ge1ha = "All causes, at least 1 ha",
               n_total_ge4ha = "All causes, at least 4 ha")

ign_rows <- list()
for (r in names(RESPONSES)) {
  for (s in names(SERIES)) {
    dcol <- paste0(s, "_fwi")
    if (!dcol %in% names(mod_dat)) next
    m <- tryCatch(ignition_model(mod_dat, r, dcol, extra = "n_stations"),
                  error = function(e) NULL)
    if (is.null(m)) next
    # Held-out skill is computed only for the two responses the comparison
    # between series is read from. It refits the model once per season, so
    # running it on all five responses costs several hundred fits for numbers
    # the text does not use, and the cost is reported rather than hidden.
    sk <- if (r %in% SKILL_RESPONSES)
      tryCatch(loso_skill(mod_dat, r, dcol), error = function(e) NULL) else NULL
    # Wald interval on the danger coefficient rather than a profile likelihood
    # one. Profiling a negative binomial with a factor per season means refitting
    # once per grid point per model, which dominated the render, and the two
    # agree closely at this sample size. The interval is reported as Wald.
    se <- summary(m)$coefficients[".x", 2]
    ci <- coef(m)[".x"] + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(0.975) * se
    ign_rows[[length(ign_rows) + 1]] <- data.frame(
      response = r, series = s,
      coef = unname(coef(m)[".x"]),
      lower = ci[1], upper = ci[2],
      p = summary(m)$coefficients[".x", 4],
      theta = m$theta,
      loso_loglik = if (is.null(sk)) NA_real_ else sk$mean_loglik,
      n_days = nrow(mod_dat))
  }
}
ign_res <- do.call(rbind, ign_rows)
write.csv(ign_res, file.path(outputs, "ignition-models.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ignition
#| tbl-cap: "Negative binomial models of daily ignition counts on daily basin Fire Weather Index, over the 1 May to 30 September window, with season as a fixed effect, two annual harmonics in day of year, and the number of contributing stations. The coefficient is the log change in expected count per unit of Fire Weather Index, identified from within-season variation only. Held-out log likelihood is the mean per day under leave-one-season-out refitting; larger is better, and the comparison between series rather than its absolute value is the quantity of interest. It is computed for the lightning and all-cause responses only, because those are the two the text compares and each refits the model once per season."
#| echo: true
it <- data.frame(
  Response = unname(RESPONSES[ign_res$response]),
  Series = unname(SERIES[ign_res$series]),
  `Coefficient` = round(ign_res$coef, 4),
  `95% Wald interval` = sprintf("%.4f to %.4f", ign_res$lower, ign_res$upper),
  `Rate ratio per 10 FWI` = round(exp(10 * ign_res$coef), 2),
  `Held-out log likelihood` = round(ign_res$loso_loglik, 4),
  check.names = FALSE)
it <- it[order(match(it$Response, unname(RESPONSES)), it$Series), ]
rownames(it) <- NULL
fmt_tbl(it)
```

```{r}
#| label: ignition-prose
#| echo: true
#| output: false
best <- ign_res[ign_res$response == "n_lightning_all", ]
best <- best[order(-best$loso_loglik), ]
skill_gap <- diff(range(best$loso_loglik))

# Does the danger term survive at every size threshold, and does it separate the
# lightning series from the person-caused control? The control matters: human
# ignition tracks population and access, so a danger signal appearing equally in
# both would point to a shared confounder rather than to fuel moisture.
sig_by_response <- tapply(ign_res$p, ign_res$response, function(p) sum(p < 0.05))
rr <- function(resp, s) {
  v <- ign_res$coef[ign_res$response == resp & ign_res$series == s]
  if (!length(v)) NA_real_ else exp(10 * v)
}
rr_light <- rr("n_lightning_all", "s3")
rr_person <- rr("n_person_all", "s3")
```

@tbl-ignition gives the models. The danger term was positive and significant at the conventional level for `r sum(ign_res$p < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)` of the `r nrow(ign_res)` response and series combinations, identified entirely from day-to-day variation inside a season.

The response that carried the signal was not the one expected. Ten units of Fire Weather Index multiplied the expected daily person-caused count by `r sprintf("%.2f", rr_person)` and the expected daily lightning count by `r sprintf("%.2f", rr_light)`, and it was the lightning term, not the person one, that failed to separate from zero. That is the reverse of the expected order until the two mechanisms are separated. A person-caused ignition needs an ignition source and a receptive fuel bed; the sources are close to constant from day to day, so whether one becomes a reported fire is largely a question of fuel moisture, which is what the index measures. A lightning-caused ignition needs a strike, and strikes are not in this model. Lightning ignitions also arrive in bursts, one storm producing many fires, which was visible in the fitted dispersion parameter, at `r sprintf("%.2f", ign_res$theta[ign_res$response == "n_lightning_all"][1])` for the lightning series against `r sprintf("%.2f", ign_res$theta[ign_res$response == "n_person_all"][1])` for the person-caused one, where a smaller value means more clustering. The person-caused series was carried as a control against a shared confounder and turned out to be the more informative response. No lightning-strike record covering the whole period was obtained, and that omission, rather than an absence of any relationship, is the most likely reason the lightning term is weak, since @magnussen2012bc, who had strike data, predicted the daily number of lightning fires in British Columbia better than the number of human-caused ones. A second reason is timing. A lightning ignition can smoulder in the duff before it is found, and @coogan2025lightning noted in agency fire records "a lag between the time a fire started and the time it was detected" [@coogan2025lightning, p. 16], so a lightning fire dated to one day may have been ignited under the danger of an earlier one.

The comparison the third question actually asked was between series, and it was small. On held-out seasons the three differed by `r sprintf("%.4f", skill_gap)` in mean log likelihood per day, with `r unname(SERIES_PROSE[best$series[1]])` first at `r sprintf("%.4f", best$loso_loglik[1])` and `r unname(SERIES_PROSE[best$series[nrow(best)]])` last at `r sprintf("%.4f", best$loso_loglik[nrow(best)])`. Over the `r format(best$n_days[1], big.mark = ",")` days in the window that was a total difference of about `r sprintf("%.1f", skill_gap * best$n_days[1])` log likelihood units, which is not a basis for preferring one series over another. @fig-ignition shows the fitted and observed relationship, in which the three curves are separated horizontally by the same level differences the threshold table reports as percentiles, and vertically by very little.

@tbl-stationarity tests whether that relationship changed across the record. The interaction between the danger term and season number is the quantity of interest, and it is reported with the caveat the record forces, that a between-season change is exactly what the ignition record's own non-stationarity could imitate.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ignition
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-dpi: 300
#| fig-cap: "Observed and fitted daily lightning ignition rate against daily basin Fire Weather Index under the three series. Points are the observed mean count in equal-count bins of the danger value; lines are the fitted negative binomial rate at the mean season and the mid-season day of year. The horizontal offsets between the three curves are the same level differences that the threshold table reports as percentiles."
# Two things are drawn and they are different. The points are the observed mean
# daily count in equal-count bins of the danger value, so each rests on the same
# number of days and the right hand tail is not one noisy observation. The curves
# are the fitted negative binomial rate, refitted here for the lightning response,
# evaluated at the mean fitted season effect and at mid-season day of year, which
# is what the model says a typical season looks like.
binned <- lapply(names(SERIES), function(s) {
  x <- mod_dat[[paste0(s, "_fwi")]]
  y <- mod_dat$n_lightning_all
  ok <- is.finite(x) & is.finite(y)
  br <- unique(quantile(x[ok], seq(0, 1, length.out = 13), na.rm = TRUE))
  bin <- cut(x[ok], br, include.lowest = TRUE)
  data.frame(x = tapply(x[ok], bin, mean), y = tapply(y[ok], bin, mean))
})
names(binned) <- names(SERIES)

mid_doy <- median(mod_dat$doy)
fitted_curve <- function(s) {
  m <- tryCatch(ignition_model(mod_dat, "n_lightning_all", paste0(s, "_fwi"),
                               extra = "n_stations"),
                error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(m)) return(NULL)
  co <- coef(m)
  cf <- function(nm) if (nm %in% names(co) && is.finite(co[[nm]])) co[[nm]] else 0
  yr_terms <- co[grepl("^\\.year", names(co))]
  grid <- seq(min(binned[[s]]$x, na.rm = TRUE), max(binned[[s]]$x, na.rm = TRUE),
              length.out = 60)
  eta <- cf("(Intercept)") + mean(c(0, yr_terms), na.rm = TRUE) + cf(".x") * grid +
    cf(".s1") * sin(2 * pi * mid_doy / 365.25) +
    cf(".c1") * cos(2 * pi * mid_doy / 365.25) +
    cf(".s2") * sin(4 * pi * mid_doy / 365.25) +
    cf(".c2") * cos(4 * pi * mid_doy / 365.25) +
    cf("n_stations") * mean(mod_dat$n_stations)
  data.frame(x = grid, y = exp(eta))
}
curves <- lapply(names(SERIES), fitted_curve)
names(curves) <- names(SERIES)

op <- par(mar = c(4, 4, 1.4, 1), mgp = c(2.4, 0.7, 0), cex = 0.8)
plot(NA,
     xlim = range(unlist(lapply(binned, `[[`, "x")), na.rm = TRUE),
     ylim = c(0, max(unlist(lapply(binned, `[[`, "y")), na.rm = TRUE) * 1.05),
     xlab = "Daily basin Fire Weather Index",
     ylab = "Mean lightning ignitions per day")
for (s in names(SERIES)) {
  points(binned[[s]]$x, binned[[s]]$y, col = cols[s], pch = 16, cex = 0.8)
  if (!is.null(curves[[s]])) lines(curves[[s]]$x, curves[[s]]$y, col = cols[s], lwd = 1.6)
}
legend("topleft", legend = unname(SERIES), col = cols, lwd = 1.6, pch = 16,
       bty = "n", cex = 0.75)
par(op)
```

```{r}
#| label: stationarity
#| echo: true
#| output: false
# Is the danger to ignition relationship stationary? The test is an interaction
# between the danger term and season number. Season is already a fixed effect,
# so the interaction asks whether the within-season slope changes over the
# record, which is a different question from whether the intercept does.
stat_rows <- list()
for (r in c("n_lightning_all", "n_total_all")) {
  for (s in names(SERIES)) {
    dcol <- paste0(s, "_fwi")
    d <- mod_dat
    d$.yc <- d$year - mean(d$year)
    m <- tryCatch(ignition_model(d, r, dcol, extra = "I(.x * .yc)"),
                  error = function(e) NULL)
    if (is.null(m)) next
    cf <- summary(m)$coefficients
    nm <- grep("I\\(.x", rownames(cf), value = TRUE)[1]
    stat_rows[[length(stat_rows) + 1]] <- data.frame(
      response = r, series = s,
      interaction = cf[nm, 1], se = cf[nm, 2], p = cf[nm, 4])
  }
}
stationarity <- do.call(rbind, stat_rows)
write.csv(stationarity, file.path(outputs, "stationarity-tests.csv"),
          row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-stationarity
#| tbl-cap: "Test of whether the within-season relationship between fire danger and daily ignition count changes across the record. The reported term is the interaction between the Fire Weather Index and centred season number; a positive value would mean more ignitions per unit danger in later seasons. Season is already a fixed effect, so this asks about the slope and not the level."
#| echo: true
st <- data.frame(
  Response = unname(RESPONSES[stationarity$response]),
  Series = unname(SERIES[stationarity$series]),
  `Interaction` = signif(stationarity$interaction, 3),
  `Standard error` = signif(stationarity$se, 3),
  `p` = signif(stationarity$p, 3),
  check.names = FALSE)
fmt_tbl(st)
```

# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

```{r}
#| label: discussion-numbers
#| echo: true
#| output: false
# The level shifts each change produces, per season, on the two absolute-threshold
# counts. Sign matters here and is computed, not asserted: the two changes do not
# necessarily push the same way.
lvl <- function(metric, a, b) {
  mean(metrics[[metric]][metrics$series == b], na.rm = TRUE) -
    mean(metrics[[metric]][metrics$series == a], na.rm = TRUE)
}
shift <- data.frame(
  metric = c("Days FFMC >= 91", "Days FWI >= 19"),
  version = c(lvl("n_ffmc_ge91", "s1", "s2"), lvl("n_fwi_ge19", "s1", "s2")),
  input = c(lvl("n_ffmc_ge91", "s2", "s3"), lvl("n_fwi_ge19", "s2", "s3")),
  migration = c(lvl("n_ffmc_ge91", "s1", "s3"), lvl("n_fwi_ge19", "s1", "s3"))
)
write.csv(shift, file.path(outputs, "level-shifts.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

same_sign <- function(i) sign(shift$version[i]) == sign(shift$input[i])
ffmc_word <- if (same_sign(1)) "compound" else "oppose one another"
fwi_word <- if (same_sign(2)) "compound" else "oppose one another"

# Where the two changes oppose, what survives is the residual, and how much
# survives is the whole point. Cancellation is measured as the migration shift
# relative to the larger of the two component shifts.
residual <- function(i) {
  abs(shift$migration[i]) / max(abs(shift$version[i]), abs(shift$input[i]))
}
ffmc_res <- residual(1); fwi_res <- residual(2)
bigger <- function(i) if (abs(shift$version[i]) > abs(shift$input[i]))
  "the version change" else "the input resolution change"
```

## Version and Input

```{r}
#| label: tbl-shift
#| tbl-cap: "How each change moves the seasonal count of extreme days, in days per season averaged over kept station-seasons. The version column is FWI1987 to FWI2025 at fixed 13:00 input; the input column is the 13:00 pathway to observed hourly weather at fixed FWI2025; the migration column is the two together, and equals their sum by construction, so the signs of the two components are what the table shows."
#| echo: true
sh <- data.frame(
  Metric = shift$metric,
  `Version change` = sprintf("%+.1f", shift$version),
  `Input resolution change` = sprintf("%+.1f", shift$input),
  `Migration, both` = sprintf("%+.1f", shift$migration),
  check.names = FALSE)
fmt_tbl(sh)
```

The reason a straight comparison of FWI1987 against FWI2025 would have been uninterpretable is in @tbl-shift, and it is not that the two changes were small, because they were large and they pointed opposite ways.

On the count of days above a Fine Fuel Moisture Code of 91, the version change moved the seasonal count by `r sprintf("%+.1f", shift$version[1])` days and the input resolution change by `r sprintf("%+.1f", shift$input[1])`, so the two `r ffmc_word`, and `r bigger(1)` won, the migration netting `r sprintf("%+.1f", shift$migration[1])` days. On the count of days above a Fire Weather Index of 19 the same two changes moved it by `r sprintf("%+.1f", shift$version[2])` and `r sprintf("%+.1f", shift$input[2])` days, so there they `r fwi_word` too, but almost exactly, the migration netting `r sprintf("%+.1f", shift$migration[2])` days, `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * fwi_res)` per cent of the larger component.

That is the case for the three-series design. A study that had computed FWI1987 on noon data and FWI2025 on hourly data would have seen `r sprintf("%+.1f", shift$migration[1])` days on one metric and `r sprintf("%+.1f", shift$migration[2])` on the other, and would have concluded that the update barely touched the Fire Weather Index count while shifting the Fine Fuel Moisture Code count. Both readings would be wrong about the mechanism, because the Fire Weather Index count was not stable through nothing happening to it but because a `r sprintf("%+.1f", shift$version[2])` day version effect and a `r sprintf("%+.1f", shift$input[2])` day input effect happened to land on top of one another in this basin. Cancellation of that kind is a coincidence of two large effects at one place rather than robustness, and there is no reason for it to hold at a site with a different diurnal range.

The mechanism is consistent with what the update did. Halving the fine fuel time lag and letting the litter dry overnight lets the Fine Fuel Moisture Code reach further at the top of the day, which is the version change, whereas replacing a reconstructed diurnal curve with the observed one lets it reach the actual extremes of the actual day rather than the average shape of a typical one, which is the input change. The first acts on the model, the second on what the model is shown, and there is no reason for them to point the same way on every index. @wastl2013large found at five Alpine stations that differences between regions were largest in the Fine Fuel Moisture Code, smaller in the Duff Moisture Code and smallest in the Drought Code, and attributed that order to the time lags of the fuel layers each code represents, so a change to the fine fuel time lag would be expected to act most strongly on the Fine Fuel Moisture Code and on the counts built from it. The Fire Weather Index combines the codes with wind, and @rodrigues2020identifying noted that the same Fire Weather Index value could arise from different combinations of weather variables, so two changes that acted on different parts of the calculation could offset in the combined index while remaining visible in its parts.

The few studies that varied one element of a fire danger calculation on a fixed record found effects of the same kind. On thirteen years of station data from Camden, New South Wales, @matthews2009comparison found that the differences in structure between three fire danger systems partly cancelled once each used its own observation time and moisture sub-models, which is the cancellation found here for days above a Fire Weather Index of 19, where a `r sprintf("%+.1f", shift$version[2])` day version effect and a `r sprintf("%+.1f", shift$input[2])` day input effect netted `r sprintf("%+.1f", shift$migration[2])` days. On the Iberian Peninsula, @herrera2013daily found that daily mean inputs missed 45 per cent of the extreme days in the series computed from 12 UTC inputs, and here replacing the reconstructed diurnal curve with observed hourly weather moved the count of days above a Fine Fuel Moisture Code of 91 by `r sprintf("%+.1f", shift$input[1])` days per season, so in both records the way the weather was supplied to the calculation moved the extreme-day count by an amount comparable to a change of system. @rodell2024hourly found in western North America that hourly Fire Weather Index values sampled at noon were biased low against the daily index because noon did not coincide with peak fire behaviour, which is the reason the daily value here was taken at 17:00 local daylight time and the daily maximum was reported only as a bound. None of those studies followed a trend through the change, so the result here that the version change moved levels far more than slopes could not be compared with any of them.

The clearest difference between the two FWI2025 series was not in any level but in the burning window, because the number of hours per day on which spread-sustaining conditions held differed substantially between the observed hourly weather and the diurnal curve reconstructed from a single noon observation. Both are FWI2025 and both are the report's own procedures, so an agency that migrates to FWI2025 while continuing to supply a 13:00 observation gets the new system's outputs computed from an assumption about the shape of the day, and the assumption is smoother than the day.

This is the part of the update that is genuinely new rather than a change of scale, because a daily index cannot say when the peak arrives or how long it lasts, and those are the two quantities an initial attack decision actually needs. The finding here was not that the hourly series predicted ignitions better, because it was barely distinguishable on that, but that it answered a question the daily series cannot be asked.

The small difference in ignition skill between the three series agreed with comparisons of danger indices against fire records elsewhere. In Mediterranean France, @castelclavera2025comparative found the Fire Weather Index the most skilful of the indices tested but found that no index alone was sufficient to rate fire activity without spatial and seasonal effects. The ignition models here carried the seasonal effect as two annual harmonics in day of year, with season as a factor, whereas a model of one basin mean had no spatial effect to carry. Skill on occurrence also did not carry over to area, because across 11 regions from the European Alps to the Mediterranean basin @bekar2023integrating found that models with a high area under the receiver operating characteristic curve for fire occurrence could still perform poorly on burned area, and @bedia2015global found across the world's major biomes a saturation threshold in the response of area burned to fire weather, above which area burned was insensitive to further increases, so the ignition counts tested here could not show whether the three series would differ on area burned. A more direct test of the halved time lag would score both versions against measured litter moisture, as @schunk2017fine did to rank danger indices in eight forest stands in southern Germany, where fire records were too sparse for that purpose.

## Published Trends

The practical consequence for the published record is narrow and specific. Trends reported as percentile exceedances, where the threshold is computed inside the series being trended, are largely insulated from the version change, because the threshold moves with the distribution. Trends reported as counts above a fixed danger class are not, and neither are seasonal severity ratings, which accumulate a transform of the index level over a season and therefore inherit any level shift. Fixed classes were already uncertain across regions before any version change, since @papagiannaki2020weather found that the Fire Weather Index class thresholds of the European Forest Fire Information System were too low for Greece and that thresholds fitted to Greek fire records predicted wildfire danger significantly better. That insulation is from the version and not from the reference period. @dunn2022reference found that warm-day trends computed from the same data over the same years changed by about 25 to 50 per cent when the percentile reference period moved, and @zhang2005percentile showed that counts outside a base period are biased upward unless the rates inside it are bootstrapped, so a percentile trend is portable across the version change only when its reference period is stated, held fixed and treated for that bias.

Nothing here says the published trends are wrong, only that they are statements about FWI1987, that restating them under FWI2025 will change some of them, and that the size of the change depends on how the metric was defined rather than on the weather. Anyone re-expressing a historical trend in the new system's units should recompute the whole record rather than splice, and should say which metric family the result belongs to.

## Limitations

```{r}
#| label: limits-compute
#| echo: true
#| output: false
# The quantitative limits statement. For each metric the minimum detectable trend
# is the slope this record could resolve at 80 per cent power, given the residual
# spread of that metric about its own Theil-Sen line. Expressing it over the whole
# window rather than per season is what makes it legible: a slope of 0.3 days per
# season is 10 days over 34 seasons, and the second number is the one a reader can
# judge.
lim <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(trends, trends$metric), function(d) {
  mdt <- median(d$mdt, na.rm = TRUE)
  data.frame(
    Metric = METRICS$label[match(d$metric[1], METRICS$col)],
    `Median observed slope` = round(median(d$slope, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    `Minimum detectable slope` = round(mdt, 3),
    `Minimum detectable change over the window` =
      round(mdt * (yr_last - yr_first), 2),
    `Observed change over the window` =
      round(median(d$slope, na.rm = TRUE) * (yr_last - yr_first), 2),
    check.names = FALSE)
}))
lim <- lim[order(match(lim$Metric, METRICS$label)), ]
rownames(lim) <- NULL
write.csv(lim, file.path(outputs, "detectability.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-limits
#| tbl-cap: "What a window of this length can and cannot resolve. The minimum detectable slope is the trend at which a two-sided test at alpha 0.05 would reach 80 per cent power given the residual spread of that metric about its own Theil-Sen line, adjusted for the efficiency of the Theil-Sen estimator relative to least squares and inflated for lag-one autocorrelation of the residuals. A metric whose observed change is smaller than its minimum detectable change is not evidence of no trend; it is evidence that this record cannot see one of that size."
#| echo: true
fmt_tbl(lim)
```

@tbl-limits is the quantitative form of what this study cannot say. It matters because a null result and an underpowered result read identically in a table of p values and are entirely different claims. Where a metric's observed change over the window fell below its minimum detectable change, the correct statement is that a trend of that size would not have been seen here, not that there is none.

Six further limits are structural rather than statistical. First, the study covered one basin, and only its Canadian part. Everything here is the Okanagan watershed group, and the United States portion of the basin was excluded because neither the ignition record nor the weather record crosses the border. Whether the version effect found here has the same size elsewhere is untested, and there is a specific reason to expect it not to, because the mechanism runs through the diurnal cycle, and the Okanagan's is unusually wide. Second, the study detected change and did not attribute it. Nothing here separated a change in fire danger from its causes, no claim was made about anthropogenic forcing, and none should be read in, because attribution requires a comparison against a world without the forcing that this design did not construct [@kirchmeieryoung2019attribution]. Third, no oscillation term entered any model. The El Niño Southern Oscillation and the Pacific Decadal Oscillation modulate fire season severity in interior British Columbia [@meyn2010oscillations], although @tan2019dynamic found that neither had contributed to wildfire weather in western Canada and that spring warming and drying there since 1871 could not be attributed to common teleconnections, and in another mountain region @mamgain2026satellite found fire danger elevated in El Niño years and reduced in La Niña years from 2000 to 2024. A window that begins and ends in different phases carries a biased slope regardless of estimator. No oscillation index was included, and including one would require choosing the index and the lag from the literature on interior British Columbia fire seasons before the record was examined. The absolute trends under the first question therefore carry that bias, whereas the comparison between series under the second does not, because all three series see the same oscillation. Fourth, fuel was held fixed. Fuel typing did not vary through time in this design, so nothing here distinguished a danger effect from fuel accumulation, which is a stated boundary and not a gap to be filled with the same data. The boundary matters for reading a danger trend as a fire trend, because @wastl2012climate found meteorological fire danger rising in Bavaria while the number of fires and the area burned fell, and @zhao2025multifactorial found across mid to high northern latitudes from 1982 to 2018 that rising flammability increased wildfire in fuel-rich forests but decreased it where water deficits had reduced fuel. Fifth, four analysis choices, the season window, the coverage threshold, the reference period and the daily summary hour, were set with the data in view rather than fixed in advance, so the absolute trends carry that freedom, whereas the comparison between series does not, because all three series ran through the same choices and a choice that moved one moved all three. Sixth, the season window was fixed. A 1 May to 30 September window measures danger inside a season of fixed length and cannot register a season that lengthens at either end, so if the true season lengthened, the counts inside the window rose by less than whole-season counts would have, and trends in window counts understate trends in the season. Four routes would recover the season from this basin, each at a cost. The first is a year-round climate station of the kind @hanes2020overwinter used for winter precipitation, driving the temperature rule of @lawson2008weather and overwintering the Drought Code, at the cost of dating the season from a valley site rather than from the fire weather stations. The second is the danger-series definition of @jolly2015global applied inside a wider fixed window, which needs the stations to be reporting before the first day above half the danger range and fails in any season they were not. The third is the fire-based definitions of @westerling2016increasing and @granville2026season, which the basin's ignition record cannot support after 2000 because its dating completeness fell, as @sec-data showed. The fourth is a reanalysis start date, which carries the grid-cell caveat set out below. The first route is the one this record could adopt, because it would also replace the Drought Code restart that @mcelhinny2020era5 showed changes spread-day counts, and it would enter all three series alike, leaving the comparison between them intact.

The obvious way to extend this study is to run it on a reanalysis, which would buy the whole basin, a longer record and every other basin in Canada at once. The reason it was not done here is stated, because it is the same reason the extension is not straightforward.

Pathway A of FWI2025 needs the timing of rainfall within the day. That is the input the halved fine fuel time lag and the six hour canopy interception reset both act on, and it is the input a once-daily observation cannot supply. Very few long records carry genuinely hourly precipitation. This basin has one because the BC Wildfire Service network was built to run a fire danger system, and its archive preserves the hourly rain gauge alongside the computed codes. A reanalysis does supply hourly precipitation, but it supplies a modelled one, and @cffdg2025fwi2025 states the caveat plainly in Appendix C-1, that "numerical weather model outputs are not strictly the same as point observations of weather from a weather station", and "At the grid cell scale, outputs from numerical models typically represent what can be thought of as average conditions across that cell." Evaluations of gridded fire danger products bear that caveat out. @bedia2012reanalysis found that the NCEP, ERA-40 and ERA-Interim reanalyses all tended to underestimate the Fire Weather Index computed at seven Spanish weather stations, @field2020gfwed found that components computed from MERRA-2 were in general biased low against a global station network, @vitolo2020era5 found the largest biases of the ERA5 fire danger reanalysis in mountainous areas, and @silver2025colorado found that station and reanalysis records in the mountains of Colorado disagreed on whether a fire weather trend existed at all. A cell average is exactly the quantity whose diurnal range is smallest, and the diurnal range is the mechanism under test here. A reanalysis-driven version comparison would therefore be biased towards finding no difference, in a basin where the relief runs through more than two kilometres.

That is a statement about this comparison, not about reanalysis in general. For estimating the level or the trend of fire danger over a region, a reanalysis is the right instrument and a five station network is not. The two questions want different data, and conflating them is how a study of one gets answered with the instrument for the other.

# Conclusions {#sec-conclusions}

```{r}
#| label: conclusions-numbers
#| echo: true
#| output: false
# The four numbers the conclusions rest on, pulled from the objects above rather
# than retyped.
c_days_gap <- d_s3 - d_s1
c_pct_gap <- 100 * c_days_gap / d_s1
c_dur <- if (exists("ct") && nrow(ct) == 2) {
  ct$`Mean burning window (h)`[grepl("S3", ct$Series)] -
    ct$`Mean burning window (h)`[grepl("S2", ct$Series)]
} else NA_real_
c_abs_rate <- sc["migration, absolute", "rate"]
c_rel_rate <- sc["migration, relative", "rate"]
```

Over `r n_seasons` seasons in the Okanagan basin the 2025 update to the Fire Weather Index System left the middle of the distribution close to where it was and moved the tail, so a level was portable across the two versions and a count of extreme days was not. The threshold the update's own report offers as the example of continuity, a Fine Fuel Moisture Code of 91, selected `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(c_days_gap))` `r if (c_days_gap >= 0) "more" else "fewer"` days per season under the new system driven by hourly weather than under the old one, a change of `r sprintf("%.0f", abs(c_pct_gap))` per cent in a quantity that is routinely trended.

Which of the two changes was responsible depended on the metric, and neither change dominated, because the version and the input resolution acted in opposite directions on some metrics and the same direction on others, which is why running the old system against the new one without separating them would have given an uninterpretable answer. That separation, not the size of any single number here, is the part of this design worth reusing.

The effect was on the level and not, so far as this record could resolve, on the slope. Under absolute thresholds the migration changed the estimated trend at `r sprintf("%.0f", c_abs_rate)` per cent of station-metric combinations and under thresholds internal to each series at `r sprintf("%.0f", c_rel_rate)` per cent, against a resolution of about `r sprintf("%.1f", res_abs * (yr_last - yr_first))` days over the window, so a trend difference smaller than that would not have been seen. What was comfortably visible was the level difference, and a level difference is enough to break a comparison between a number published under the old system and a number computed under the new one, even where both are trending at the same rate.

The practical recommendation follows from the level result and costs nothing to adopt. Fire danger trends should be reported as exceedances of a percentile computed inside the series being reported, over a stated and fixed reference period and with the base-period bias removed, not as counts above a fixed danger class, and the report should state which, because a percentile threshold moves with the distribution it is drawn from and is therefore portable across the version change, whereas a fixed class boundary is not.

For predicting where fires start, the three series were close to interchangeable in this basin. What the hourly system added was not accuracy in the daily number but information the daily number cannot carry, namely when in the day the peak arrives and how long the burning window stays open, and on that second quantity the observed hourly weather and the reconstructed diurnal curve disagreed by `r if (is.finite(c_dur)) sprintf("%.1f hours per day", c_dur) else "an amount this run did not compute"`. An agency migrating to FWI2025 with only a 13:00 observation to feed it would inherit that disagreement without any sign of it in the output.

None of this is attribution. It is a measurement of how much a published Canadian fire danger trend depends on the arithmetic that produced it, made in one basin where the weather record was good enough to ask.

#| label: abstract

# Composed with sprintf from objects the document already computed. Nothing here

# fails, which is the point.
pull <- function(d, s, col) d[[col]][grepl(toupper(s), d$Series)]

abs_ffmc <- subset(tp, Component == "FFMC" & Threshold == 91)
abs_p <- vapply(c("S1", "S2", "S3"), function(s)
  pull(abs_ffmc, s, "Percentile of threshold"), numeric(1))
abs_d <- vapply(c("S1", "S2", "S3"), function(s)
  pull(abs_ffmc, s, "Days per season above"), numeric(1))

# The migration contrast, absolute against relative thresholding.
mig_rows <- sdiff[sdiff$contrast == mig_label, ]
abs_mig <- mig_rows[mig_rows$scheme == "absolute", ]
rel_mig <- mig_rows[mig_rows$scheme == "relative", ]
n_abs_sig <- sum(abs_mig$lower > 0 | abs_mig$upper < 0, na.rm = TRUE)
n_rel_sig <- sum(rel_mig$lower > 0 | rel_mig$upper < 0, na.rm = TRUE)

# Ignition skill, on the lightning series.
lig <- ign_res[ign_res$response == "n_lightning_all", ]
lig <- lig[order(-lig$loso_loglik), ]

abstract_text <- sprintf(
"Almost every published Canadian fire danger trend is expressed in the units of
the 1987 Fire Weather Index System, which the Canadian Forest Service replaced in
2025 with a version that changed the calculation and the resolution of the
weather driving it at once, so a straight comparison cannot attribute a
difference to either change, and no study has separated them. This study
computed three danger series from one hourly weather record (%d fire weather
stations, %s station-seasons, %d fire seasons, %d to %d, Canadian Okanagan basin,
British Columbia), FWI1987 from the 13:00 observation, FWI2025 from the same
observation through the legacy pathway, and FWI2025 from observed hourly weather.
Trends were estimated with the Theil-Sen slope and the Mann-Kendall test under
the Hamed and Rao correction, series differences were bootstrapped over blocks of
consecutive seasons, and daily ignition counts were modelled as negative binomial with
season as a fixed effect. The comparability claimed by the 2025 report held for
levels and failed for tails, in that a Fine Fuel Moisture Code of 91 sat at percentile
%.1f of the legacy series and percentile %.1f of the hourly series, %.0f
against %.0f days per season. Of %d station-metric combinations under absolute
thresholds, %d gave a migration slope difference excluding zero, against %d of
%d under percentile thresholds, at a resolution of about %.1f days over the
window, so the version change was a shift in level rather than in slope. On
held-out seasons the three series differed by %.4f in mean log likelihood per
day, %s. Fire danger trends should therefore be reported as percentile
exceedances with the version of the System stated, because a fixed danger class
did not carry across the change and a percentile threshold did.\n",
  n_stations_kept, format(n_kept, big.mark = ","), n_seasons, yr_first, yr_last,
  abs_p[["S1"]], abs_p[["S3"]], abs_d[["S1"]], abs_d[["S3"]],
  nrow(abs_mig), n_abs_sig, n_rel_sig, nrow(rel_mig),
  res_abs * (yr_last - yr_first),
  diff(range(lig$loso_loglik)),
  sprintf("with %s ranking first", unname(SERIES_PROSE[lig$series[1]]))
)
cat(abstract_text)
cat("\n**Keywords:** fire danger; Canadian Forest Fire Weather Index System;",
    "FWI2025; trend detection; Theil-Sen; Okanagan; British Columbia\n")
